The anxiety disorders are told apart by one question: what is the fear about? Panic, generalized anxiety and social anxiety are the three the lecture asks you to compare.
1. Fear vs anxiety

• Fear = an intense reaction to an immediate threat - it saves your life now
  • Anxiety = a negative emotion about the possibility of a future threat - it saves your life later · drives hypervigilance, worry and avoidance
  • Risk factors
    • family history · personal history of anxiety, mood disorders or attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
    • childhood trauma · female sex · chronic medical illness (asthma, diabetes, obesity, heart disease)
    • behavioural inhibition (a temperament reluctant to approach new things)
  • 7 disorders in the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, 5th edition), remembered as GPS-MAPS: Generalized · Panic · Social · selective Mutism · Agoraphobia · specific Phobia · Separation anxiety
    • the first three matter most · selective mutism and separation anxiety are lower yield
2. The five to compare

rows: Excessive, uncontrollable worry most days + 3 of 6: restless · tired · poor concentration · irritable · muscle tension · poor sleep (only 1 needed in children)
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) · selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI): escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine · also venlafaxine, pregabalin, buspirone
The panic attacks themselves and their consequences
2+ unexpected (untriggered) panic attacks + worry about more attacks or a change in behaviour to avoid them
Worry or behaviour change for 1+ month after an attack
CBT with interoceptive exposure · SSRI (also venlafaxine)
Being somewhere escape or help is hard if panic starts
Fear of 2 of 5: public transport · open spaces · enclosed spaces · crowds or lines · being outside home alone
As for panic disorder (often occur together)
Fear of scrutiny in social or performance situations (talking, eating in front of others, speeches) · specifier: performance only
CBT with exposure · SSRI (also fluvoxamine, venlafaxine, pregabalin)
Fear out of proportion, almost always triggered, avoided · types: animal · natural environment · blood-injection-injury · situational
Exposure therapy · short-term benzodiazepine to get through an exposure

blocks.html:
• The 6-month rule covers every one of them except panic disorder, where it is 1 month of worry after an attack
  • Blood-injection-injury phobia is the odd one out: blood pressure and heart rate drop (vasovagal response, fainting) instead of rising
  • A fear is only a phobia when it impairs function
3. Panic attacks and panic disorder

• Panic attack = an abrupt surge of fear that peaks within minutes, with 4 or more of 13 symptoms
    • body: palpitations · sweating · trembling · shortness of breath · choking · chest pain · nausea · dizziness · chills or hot flashes · numbness or tingling
    • mind: derealization or depersonalization · fear of losing control · fear of dying
  • A panic attack is a symptom that can occur in any anxiety disorder; panic disorder needs attacks that come out of the blue
  • Do not just ask "do you have panic attacks?" - ask for a sudden rush of fear with no obvious cause, and have them describe it
  • Rule out medical and substance causes
    • endocrine: hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism · low blood sugar · pheochromocytoma
    • heart and lungs: arrhythmia · coronary disease · heart failure · asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
    • other: anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency · migraine, brain tumour · caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stimulants
    • bloodwork: complete blood count · glucose · electrolytes · liver enzymes · thyroid-stimulating hormone · creatinine · B12 · urinalysis
  • Epidemiology: 5% lifetime · 30-50% also have agoraphobia · more common in women · starts in late adolescence · often with depression · suicide risk about 20 times the general population
4. Telling them apart

blocks.html:
• Panic vs social anxiety: panic fears the bodily symptoms · social anxiety fears other people's judgement (panic attacks may occur, but only in social situations)
  • GAD vs depression: many symptoms overlap and they often occur together · separate them by the timeline and prominent low mood in depression
  • Social anxiety vs avoidant personality disorder: avoidant personality is broader, with lower self-esteem · social anxiety is tied to particular situations
  • Social anxiety vs paranoid personality: paranoid people believe others are critical · socially anxious people worry they might be
  • Claustrophobia vs agoraphobia: claustrophobia fears being enclosed · agoraphobia fears panic symptoms with no escape

lectures.name: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
lectures.title: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ First-line OCD treatment is exposure and response prevention plus an SSRI at a higher-than-depression dose for 8-12 weeks; after 2 failed SSRIs, switch to clomipramine. Diagnosis needs more than 1 hour a day or real distress. OCD is ego-dystonic; obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is ego-syntonic. Insight is graded good, poor or absent; absent insight (4%) predicts a worse course and may need an antipsychotic add-on. GAD worries are about real-life events; obsessions are intrusive and themed.

An obsession raises anxiety; a compulsion brings it down for a moment and so keeps the cycle going. Most people have some intrusive thoughts and rituals - OCD is the version that eats time and causes distress.
1. Obsessions and compulsions

• Obsession = a recurrent, persistent thought, urge or image that feels intrusive and unwanted (ego-dystonic) and causes marked anxiety
    • the person tries to ignore, suppress or neutralize it
    • common themes: contamination · symmetry · aggression or harm · somatic · religious · sexual
  • Compulsion = a repetitive behaviour (washing, ordering, checking) or mental act (praying, counting, repeating words) done in response to an obsession or by rigid rules
    • aims to prevent harm or reach a "just right" feeling
    • not realistically connected to what it is meant to prevent, or clearly excessive
  • Hallmarks: excessive doubt and intolerance of uncertainty
  • 96% have both obsessions and compulsions
  • Normal is common: about 80% of people have obsessions and 55% have compulsions · in OCD the thoughts carry more weight, are harder to dismiss, and compulsions become the learned way to relieve them
2. Diagnosis

• Criteria
    • obsessions, compulsions or both
    • time-consuming (more than 1 hour a day) or causing clinically significant distress or impairment
    • not due to a substance or medical condition · not better explained by another mental disorder
  • Insight specifier
    • good or fair: knows the beliefs are definitely or probably untrue
    • poor: thinks they are probably true
    • absent or delusional: completely convinced (4%, worse outcome)
  • Tic-related specifier: current or past tic disorder (30% have one, mostly men with childhood onset)
  • Screening questions: unpleasant thoughts you cannot get rid of? · worry you might act on an impulse and harm someone? · counting, washing or checking over and over?
  • Severity scale: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale
3. Epidemiology and course

• 2-3% lifetime · 60% women (pregnancy and postpartum raise the risk) · one-third severe
  • Median onset 19 years · 21% start in childhood, more often boys
  • 90% have another mental disorder (anxiety 76%, mood disorders)
  • Core symptoms look the same across cultures
  • Course: waxing and waning (better) or constant (worse)
  • Worse prognosis: early onset · giving in to compulsions · bizarre compulsions · hospitalization · comorbid depression · poor insight or delusions · schizotypal personality
4. Telling OCD apart

rows: Worries about real everyday events, felt as reasonable (ego-syntonic), almost always thoughts, not resisted as hard · obsessions are intrusive, on specific themes, and can be images
Beliefs always of delusional intensity and ego-syntonic · OCD insight is often intact at times, and antipsychotics can worsen OCD
Focus is only on appearance, with shame and low self-esteem
Driven by acquiring and distress at discarding, not by an obsession · OCD hoarding is unwanted
Worry is only about illness, from misreading body sensations
Giving in to the urge is pleasurable · OCD compulsions only relieve anxiety
Ego-syntonic, no insight, little distress (perfectionism, rigidity, trouble discarding, tight spending) · only 25% of people with OCD also have it

blocks.html: 5. Treatment

• Psychotherapy: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
    • exposure to the cue that triggers the obsession
    • response prevention: resist the compulsion so the anxiety fades on its own (habituation)
    • cognitive work on: thought-action fusion ("thinking it makes it more likely") · overvaluing thoughts · intolerance of uncertainty · emotional reasoning · inflated responsibility
  • Medication
    • first line: SSRIs - paroxetine, fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram
    • doses are higher than for depression · a fair trial is 8-12 weeks
    • continue 6 months to 2 years after response; some need it for life

• Refractory = 3 failed SSRIs + failed add-on + failed CBT combined with medication
  • Outcomes: 20-30% improve a lot · 40-50% moderately · 20-40% little or not at all

lectures.name: Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD
lectures.title: Management of anxiety disorders and OCD
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ First line for every anxiety disorder, OCD and PTSD is CBT plus an SSRI - escitalopram, sertraline or paroxetine ("ESP"). Interoceptive exposure is the one for panic disorder; imaginal exposure is the one for PTSD. Exposure must be planned, predictable, prolonged, paced and practised - and the quick fix (escape) undoes it. Benzodiazepines are short-term only: to get through a phobia exposure, or SSRI restlessness. Pregabalin when SSRIs are contraindicated, as in bipolar disorder. Clomipramine is OCD-only.

Two first-line treatments cover every anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): an SSRI and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) built around exposure.
1. Medications

• First line almost across the board - "ESP": escitalopram · sertraline · paroxetine (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, SSRIs)
  • Which drug for which disorder:

• Benzodiazepines: the only listed use is specific phobia, short term, to get through an exposure
  • Pregabalin (not an SSRI): for when SSRIs are contraindicated (e.g. bipolar disorder) or several SSRI trials have failed · also helps pain
  • Clomipramine is for OCD only, after 2 SSRIs fail
2. SSRI side effects - "SSRIS"

rows: A short course of a benzodiazepine

blocks.html: 3. Cognitive behavioural therapy

• CBT is first line for every anxiety disorder, OCD and PTSD
  • Changes both thoughts and behaviours - the patient learns to think and act differently from what the anxiety demands
  • Thinking errors it targets: probability overestimation · catastrophizing · intolerance of uncertainty
4. Exposure therapy

• Face the feared thing until the anxiety falls on its own · each repeat starts lower and falls faster
  • Do not take the "quick fix" (escaping, distraction, safety behaviours, compulsions) - it relieves anxiety now and keeps it going
  • The 5 P's: planned · predictable and structured · prolonged (until anxiety drops naturally) · paced (gradual) · practised often and close together

blocks.alt: exposure fear curve one vs many exposures - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Fear peaks and falls during one exposure; after many exposures the peak is small and brief - escaping early (the quick fix) stops that from happening

rows: Social anxiety: eat at a window seat · panic: crowded subway · OCD: touch an elevator button · phobia: drive over a bridge
Bring on the body sensation that is feared
Racing heart: spin, run on the spot · breathlessness: breathe through a straw · derealization: stare in a mirror · heat: hot drink, stuffy car
Situation plus the feared sensations - faces the whole fear
Hyperventilate in a car · wear a sweater to give a talk · hold your breath in an elevator

blocks.html:
• Social anxiety: face the feared outcome, not just the situation - a talk that goes well teaches less than one that goes wrong
    • shake on purpose during a speech · mispronounce a word · pause too long · spill food in a restaurant · ask directions to an obvious place

lectures.name: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
lectures.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ PTSD needs a criterion-A trauma, then intrusion (1+), avoidance (1+), negative mood and thinking (2+) and arousal (2+) for more than 1 month; 3 days to 1 month is acute stress disorder. Delayed expression = criteria not met until 6+ months after. First-line drugs: fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine; prazosin for nightmares. Debriefing does not prevent PTSD. Imaginal exposure is the exposure type for PTSD.

PTSD = a real trauma, then four symptom clusters - intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and thinking, and arousal - lasting more than a month. The clock (days vs a month vs 6 months) separates it from its neighbours.
1. The trauma (criterion A)

• Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, in one or more ways:
    • directly experiencing it
    • witnessing it happen to others, in person
    • learning it happened to a close family member or friend (must be violent or accidental)
    • repeated or extreme exposure to its details (first responders, police) - not through media unless it is work
2. The four symptom clusters

rows: Intrusive memories · nightmares · flashbacks (dissociative reactions) · distress at reminders · body reactions to reminders (palpitations, dizziness)
Avoids memories, thoughts or feelings about it · avoids external reminders (people, places, conversations)

Cannot recall key parts (dissociative amnesia) · negative beliefs about self, others, the world · distorted blame of self or others · persistent fear, anger, guilt or shame · lost interest · detachment · cannot feel positive emotions
Irritability, angry outbursts · reckless or self-destructive behaviour · hypervigilance · exaggerated startle · poor concentration · poor sleep

blocks.html:
• All must start or worsen after the event, last more than 1 month, cause distress or impairment, and not be due to a substance or medical condition
  • Specifiers
    • with dissociative symptoms: depersonalization (detached from your body) or derealization (things feel unreal)
    • with delayed expression: full criteria not met until 6+ months after the event
3. Timing and the differential

rows: Stressor not severe enough, or not all PTSD criteria met
Symptoms only 3 days to 1 month after the trauma
Intrusive thoughts not tied to a trauma
Arousal and dissociation not tied to a trauma
Worry about a perceived future threat, not a past event

blocks.html: 4. Who gets it

• 76% of Canadians have had a traumatic event · 9.2% lifetime PTSD · more common in women
  • Starts at any age, usually within 3 months · often follows acute stress disorder · lasts 3 months to years · flares with reminders, new trauma or failing health
  • Suicide risk 2-3 times the general population
  • 80% more likely to have another mental disorder: depression · anxiety · substance use · borderline personality disorder
  • Risk factors
    • before: prior mental illness · low income, family problems · female, younger age
    • during: severity of the event · perceived threat · dissociation that persists
    • after: negative coping · acute stress disorder · repeated reminders · further bad life events
5. Treatment

• Psychotherapy - aims at fear, loss and moral injury
    • eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR): bilateral stimulation (eyes or hands) while holding the memory · first line, though some evidence is against it
    • cognitive processing therapy: cognitive work plus written accounts · first line · an adapted version (a forgiving authority figure) for moral injury
    • prolonged exposure: imaginal or in vivo, equally effective
    • trauma-focused CBT for children 3-18
    • dialectical behaviour therapy when borderline personality coexists - reduces self-harm
    • ⚠ Psychological debriefing right after a trauma does not help and may do harm
  • Medication
    • first line: fluoxetine · paroxetine · sertraline · venlafaxine
    • second line: fluvoxamine · mirtazapine · phenelzine
    • nightmares: prazosin 2-12 mg at bedtime (a blood pressure drug) · nabilone (synthetic THC) at bedtime, "50-100 mg" in both notes - check the unit on the slides · SSRIs cut rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which may reduce nightmares
    • to avoid: alprazolam, clonazepam · citalopram · desipramine · divalproex · olanzapine · tiagabine

lectures.name: Personality Disorders
lectures.title: Personality disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Cluster A is odd (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), B is dramatic (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic), C is anxious (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive) - and no drug is approved for any of them. Dialectical behaviour therapy is the treatment for borderline personality disorder. Antisocial needs age 18+ and conduct disorder before 15. Schizoid doesn't want people; avoidant wants them but fears rejection; schizotypal is odd. Obsessive-compulsive personality is ego-syntonic; OCD is ego-dystonic. Splitting = borderline; projection = paranoid.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

A personality disorder is a lifelong, inflexible way of thinking, feeling and relating that causes distress or impairment. Sort it into a cluster first (odd, dramatic or anxious), then find the one feature that names the disorder.
1. What makes it a personality disorder

• An enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that:
    • deviates markedly from the person's culture
    • is pervasive and inflexible
    • starts in adolescence or early adulthood and is stable over time (tends to soften with age)
    • causes distress or impairment
  • Shows in 2 or more of: cognition (how you see yourself and others) · affect (range, intensity, fit of emotions) · interpersonal functioning · impulse control
  • Not explained by another mental disorder, a substance or a medical condition
  • Under 18: traits must be present at least 1 year · antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before 18
2. The three clusters

rows: Odd, eccentric, withdrawn · brief stress psychosis possible

blocks.html:
• Other diagnoses: personality change due to another medical condition (labile, disinhibited, aggressive, apathetic, paranoid) · other specified · unspecified
  • Prevalence: any personality disorder 11% · clusters A and B 3.5%, cluster C 6.5%
    • most common: borderline (28% of cases), then dependent (15%) and avoidant
    • strongly linked to impairment, slower recovery, worse physical health and mortality, and more health care use
3. The ten disorders

rows: Distrust - others' motives seen as malevolent (4+ of 7)
Suspects exploitation · bears grudges · doubts partner's fidelity · no fixed delusion and not acutely psychotic
Detached - neither wants nor enjoys relationships (4+ of 7)
Cold, solitary, indifferent to praise or criticism · not odd, and content alone
Eccentric - odd beliefs and perceptions, discomfort in relationships
Magical thinking, ideas of reference, odd speech and dress · social anxiety from paranoid fears · 30-50% also depressed
Disregard for others' rights since age 15 (3+ of 7)
Age 18+ with conduct disorder before 15 · deceit, lawbreaking, no remorse · men far more
Peer group therapy · behavioural therapy, CBT · SSRI or mood stabilizer for aggression
Instability of relationships, self-image and mood + impulsivity (5+ of 9)
Frantic fear of abandonment · splitting (idealize then devalue) · self-harm · chronic emptiness · stress-related paranoia or dissociation · 75% women · suicide 8-10%
Dialectical behaviour therapy · SSRI or mood stabilizer for comorbid conditions
Must be the centre of attention · seductive · uses appearance · vague, impressionistic speech · suggestible · thinks relationships closer than they are
Grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy (5+ of 9)
Wants relationships but is too afraid of rejection
Supportive · assertiveness training · beta blockers for anxiety symptoms
Needs to be taken care of - submissive, clingy, fears separation (5+ of 8)
Cannot decide alone · will not disagree · urgently finds a new carer when a relationship ends · women more
CBT · assertiveness training · family therapy · SSRIs
Orderliness, perfectionism, control at the cost of flexibility (4+ of 8)
Perfectionism stops tasks being finished · rigid, devoted to work, will not delegate, miserly · ego-syntonic (no insight) · one of the commonest in the community · men about twice as often
Isolation of affect · intellectualization · undoing · rationalization

blocks.html: • Schizotypal threshold (sources differ: the upper-year notes say 5 or more of 9 features, the medwiki condition note says 4 or more - check the slides)
4. Pairs that get confused

• Schizoid vs schizotypal vs avoidant: schizoid does not want people · schizotypal is odd (magical thinking) · avoidant wants people but fears rejection
  • Paranoid personality vs paranoid schizophrenia or delusional disorder: no fixed delusion, not acutely psychotic - the suspiciousness is part of the personality
  • Avoidant personality vs social anxiety disorder: avoidant has lower self-esteem and broader inadequacy · social anxiety is tied to particular situations
  • Obsessive-compulsive personality vs OCD: personality = ego-syntonic, no insight · OCD = ego-dystonic, knows it is not normal
  • Schizoid vs autism spectrum disorder: autism has more impaired social interaction, stereotyped behaviour and fixed interests
5. Problems with the category model

• Disorders overlap heavily · traits are more stable than diagnoses · wide variation within one label · clinicians avoid the diagnosis (stigma)
  • Overall severity is the best predictor of present and future dysfunction
  • Alternative (dimensional) model: ① moderate or severe impairment in self or interpersonal functioning + ② 1 or more pathological traits - negative affect · detachment · antagonism · disinhibition · psychoticism
6. Treatment principles

• No medication is approved for personality disorders - treat comorbid conditions (depression, anxiety) with the usual drugs
  • Psychotherapy is the treatment of choice, though the alliance can be hard to build
  • Cluster A: rarely seek help and struggle to trust a therapist · CBT if an alliance forms · antipsychotics have some evidence in schizotypal
  • Cluster B
    • borderline - the most researched, and highly treatable: dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) first line (acceptance + change, CBT, mindfulness) · mentalization-based treatment · transference-focused therapy · schema-focused therapy · good psychiatric management
    • borderline is often over-medicated - "skills not pills"
  • Cluster C: CBT and psychodynamic therapy have the strongest effects · drop-out is a problem in obsessive-compulsive and avoidant · dependent patients stay longer in treatment

lectures.name: Dissociation and Dissociative Disorders
lectures.title: Dissociation and dissociative disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Depersonalization-derealization keeps reality testing intact - that is what separates it from psychosis. Dissociative identity disorder = 2+ personality states plus recurrent gaps in everyday memory, with childhood abuse in about 90%. Dissociative amnesia is for autobiographical information, usually localized; fugue is its travel specifier. Dissociation also appears in borderline personality (stress-related), PTSD (dissociative subtype) and panic attacks. Rule out seizures, head injury, substances and transient global amnesia first.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Dissociation is a symptom first and a disorder only sometimes. Faced with it, rule out substances, seizures and psychosis, check for trauma, panic and borderline personality, and only then call it a dissociative disorder.
1. What dissociation is

• A disruption or discontinuity in the normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, movement and behaviour
  • A spectrum: from ordinary absorption (lost in a book) to severe, disabling states
  • Dissociative Experiences Scale (Dissociative Experiences Scale II): 28 questions, scored out of 100 · non-clinical average about 11
2. Disorders where dissociation is a symptom

• Borderline personality disorder: transient, stress-related severe dissociation (or paranoia)
  • Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): the dissociative subtype (depersonalization, derealization) · flashbacks are dissociative reactions · amnesia for parts of the trauma
  • Panic disorder: derealization or depersonalization during a panic attack
  • Research links it to schizophrenia, eating disorders, mood disorders and obsessive-compulsive disorder
3. The dissociative disorders - dissociation is the main problem

rows: Cannot recall important personal information, usually traumatic or stressful, beyond normal forgetting

Types: localized (a period of time - most common) · selective (parts of it) · generalized (whole life and identity - very rare) · systematized (a category) · continuous (each new event) · specifier: dissociative fugue (purposeful travel or bewildered wandering) · lasts minutes to years
Seizures, transient global amnesia, head injury, substances, dementia
2 or more distinct personality states with breaks in sense of self and agency
Recurrent gaps in memory for everyday events · may hear voices (a child, a spiritual being) · often with amnesia and fugue · childhood abuse or neglect in about 90%
A cultural or religious practice · a child's imaginary playmate · intoxication blackouts · complex partial seizures
Persistent or recurrent depersonalization (detached, watching yourself from outside) and/or derealization (surroundings unreal, foggy, time distorted)
Reality testing stays intact - not psychotic · episodes last moments or recur over years · can look like a panic attack
Schizophrenia, panic disorder, depression, PTSD or acute stress disorder

blocks.html: • Treatment named in the notes: trauma-informed psychotherapy for dissociative identity disorder
4. Approach to a patient with dissociation
• Also on the differential for amnesia: factitious disorder and malingering · catatonia · normal age-related memory change

lectures.name: Approach to ADHD
lectures.title: Approach to ADHD
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ ADHD needs 6 symptoms (5 if 17+) for 6 months, onset before 12, in 2+ settings, with impairment - and a checklist alone is never enough. Long-acting stimulants are first line and work at once; atomoxetine and guanfacine are second line. Rule out hearing, vision, thyroid, low blood sugar, lead, sleep problems and absence seizures. Girls present inattentive and are missed. Stimulants unmask tics but do not cause them; check heart rate and blood pressure. Treating ADHD lowers, not raises, substance use.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heritable brain disorder diagnosed on history from several sources - not on a checklist alone. Confirm the criteria, rule out the mimics, then treat: stimulants first, non-stimulants second, behavioural support throughout.
1. What ADHD is

• A neurodevelopmental disorder - an illness (harmful dysfunction), not bad parenting, television or video games
    • smaller or less active prefrontal cortex (executive function), limbic system (memory, emotion regulation) and basal ganglia (planning, reward, motivation)
  • Highly heritable - genetic coefficient 0.76 · polygenic
    • affected: 25-35% of siblings · 78-92% of identical twins · 20-54% of children of a parent with ADHD
  • About 20% acquired
    • prenatal: maternal smoking or alcohol (risk ×2.5) · prematurity, especially with brain bleeding (45% get ADHD) · pregnancy complications
    • after birth: head injury, hypoxia, tumour, infection · lead poisoning in the preschool years · surviving acute lymphoblastic leukemia (its treatment injures the brain)
  • The most common neurodevelopmental disorder: 5-12% of children · boys 4:1 in the community, 9:1 in clinics (referral bias) · under 2:1 in adults
    • girls more often inattentive, less disruptive, and are missed
  • Persists into adulthood in about 60%
2. Diagnostic criteria (DSM-5)

rows: Careless mistakes · cannot sustain attention · seems not to listen · does not finish tasks · disorganized · avoids sustained mental effort · loses things · easily distracted · forgetful
Fidgets · leaves seat · runs or climbs (restlessness in adults) · cannot play quietly · "on the go, driven by a motor" · talks excessively · blurts out answers · cannot wait turn · interrupts
Procrastination · slow, inefficient · poor time management · trouble in meetings and paperwork
Inner restlessness · workaholic · overscheduled · picks very active jobs · impulsivity: quits jobs, ends relationships, drives too fast

blocks.html:
• Plus all of:
    • 6+ months
    • several symptoms before age 12
    • present in 2 or more settings (home, school, work, friends)
    • clear impairment - without impairment there is no diagnosis
    • not better explained by another disorder, and not only during psychosis
  • Subtypes: inattentive (formerly "ADD") · hyperactive-impulsive · combined · specifiers: partial remission · mild, moderate, severe
  • ADHD is inconsistent attention, not zero attention - worst on tasks that are not fun or easy
3. Approach

school, work or behaviour problems"] --> B["History from several sources
parent + teacher + report cards · development · family history"] B --> C["Rating scales
SNAP-IV (parent, teacher) · Weiss functional impairment · adult self-report scale"] C --> D{"6+ symptoms in a domain (5 if 17+)
6 months · before 12 · 2+ settings · impairment?"} D -->|No| E["Not ADHD
look for another cause"] D -->|Yes| F{"Mimic or better explanation?

lead · sleep · seizures · mood, anxiety · learning disorder"} F -->|Yes| G["Treat that - ADHD may still coexist"] F -->|No| H["ADHD - name the subtype
screen comorbidities · check heart health"] H --> I["Psychoeducation + parent training

methylphenidate or amphetamine based"] J --> K{"Side effects, poor response,
or no access?"} K -->|No| L["Continue every day, all year

blocks.html:
• Ask about settings, not symptoms: "what is homework like in the evening?" rather than "is your child easily distracted?" · "what is it like to take your child shopping?"
  • Collateral history matters: adults recall their own childhood symptoms poorly
  • Check current intellectual functioning and achievement - a full psychoeducational assessment only if a learning disorder is suspected
  • Mostly assessed and treated in primary care; comorbidities may need a specialist
4. What to rule out

• Medical: hearing or vision loss · hyper- or hypothyroidism (thyroid-stimulating hormone) · low blood sugar (glucose) · anemia (complete blood count) · lead (blood lead level) · head injury · absence seizures · sleep problems including obstructive sleep apnea · fragile X, fetal alcohol syndrome, phenylketonuria, neurofibromatosis · intellectual disability
  • Psychiatric: anxiety · depression (a drop in mood vs ADHD's lifelong demoralization) · bipolar (episodic, grandiose) · oppositional defiant and conduct disorders · learning disorder · autism (30-70% also meet ADHD criteria) · personality disorders · substance use
  • Comorbidity is the rule: only 25-40% have "simple" ADHD · commonest: oppositional defiant disorder · conduct disorder · mood · anxiety · learning disorders · substance use
5. Medication

rows: Methylphenidate (Concerta, Biphentin, Foquest; short-acting Ritalin) · amphetamine based (Adderall, Vyvanse, Dexedrine)
Atomoxetine (reuptake inhibitor) · guanfacine extended release (alpha-2A agonist)
Release catecholamines and block their reuptake → more dopamine and norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex
Atomoxetine blocks reuptake · guanfacine boosts prefrontal signalling
High (sources differ: 90% in the medwiki note, 75% in the upper-year notes - check the slides)
Less appetite · insomnia · mood or anxiety, agitation · flattened affect · ↑ heart rate and blood pressure · can unmask tics · rarely hallucinations, cardiac death
Atomoxetine: stomach upset, irritability, fatigue · guanfacine: sleepiness, dizziness, dry mouth

blocks.html:
• Long-acting forms are preferred: fewer side effects, less misuse, more convenient
  • Tics: stimulants unmask them, they do not cause them - continue if not disruptive
  • Recommended 7 days a week, 12 months a year - ADHD affects social life and safety, not just school
  • Medication alone, or with behavioural treatment, reduces core symptoms (MTA study: about 6000 children over 14 months)
  • Where clonidine and bupropion sit (sources differ: second line in the upper-year notes, third-line off label in the medwiki note - check the slides)
6. Non-drug treatment

• Psychoeducation and dispelling myths ("boys will be boys", "my neighbour's kid was a zombie")
  • Parent training: agree as caregivers · externalize time (timers), information (notes) and motivation (tokens, rewards) · immediate, frequent feedback · touch more, talk less · act, don't yak · reward the good behaviour first, add mild consequences after a week · anticipate problem settings · keep a disability perspective
  • Child: behaviour modification · SNAP (Stop Now And Plan) · CBT for adults
  • School: organized assignment book · break work into chunks · desk placement · movement breaks, allow some fidgeting · daily behaviour report card · an educational assistant if needed · close parent-teacher contact
  • Why treat: untreated ADHD → 3-4× health care costs, injuries · more substance use (treatment lowers it) · teen pregnancy · arrests · 3 fewer years of education · low self-esteem

lectures.name: Speech and Language Disorders
lectures.title: Speech and language disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Language is the symbol system (what is said and understood); speech is making the sounds - and every workup starts with a hearing test. By age 3 a child should be 90% intelligible to strangers. Only 40-50% of late talkers catch up - don't wait and see. Apraxia = planning problem with inconsistent errors; dysarthria = muscle problem with drooling. Stuttering is normal at 2-4 years; treat if it lasts over 6 months, runs in the family, or bothers the child. Social communication disorder can only be diagnosed once autism is ruled out.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

First decide whether the problem is language (the symbol system - what is said and understood) or speech (making the sounds - what you hear). Whichever it is, check hearing first and refer to a speech-language pathologist.
1. Communication, language, speech

• Communication = any verbal or nonverbal behaviour that influences others - sending and receiving a message
  • Language = conventional symbols (words, signs, writing, pictures) used by rules - a symbol system
    • form: phonology (sound system) · morphology (units of meaning, like the "s" in cookies) · syntax (grammar)
    • content: semantics (meaning) · use: pragmatics (social rules)
    • expressive (producing a message) vs receptive (understanding one)
  • Speech = producing the sounds - articulation · fluency · voice · resonance - making the oral signal

blocks.alt: communication disorders classification tree - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Communication disorders: language (developmental, acquired), speech (articulation, voice, fluency) and other (swallowing, social communication, literacy)

blocks.html: 2. When to worry

• Red flags: milestones not met · parents are concerned · struggling at school with no clear reason, or behaviour problems · child cannot be understood as expected · social difficulties
  • How common: language disorders 5-10% (sources differ: 7% in the upper-year notes, 2-5% in the medwiki condition note - check the slides) · articulation 2-3% (falls with age) · voice 3% · fluency 1% (higher in preschoolers)

rows: Loud tuneful vocalizing · turns to a familiar voice
Responds to name · babbles, consonant sounds · purposeful gestures · understands "no", "bye-bye"
First words with meaning · points · follows simple one-step directions
Single words, mostly nouns (sources differ: 6-20 words in the medwiki note, at least 20 in the upper-year notes - check the slides) · points to body parts
3-word sentences · pronouns, plurals, past tense · 90% intelligible to strangers · a stutter is common

blocks.html:
• Do not "wait and see" in boys: the sex difference is only months · only 40-50% of late talkers catch up on their own
  • Bilingual children show the same pattern in both languages - a true disorder shows in all of them
3. Language disorders

• Developmental language disorder (DSM-5 language disorder)
    • persistent difficulty learning and using language: small vocabulary · limited sentence structure · poor discourse (connecting sentences)
    • well below age expectations, with functional limits · onset in early development · not due to hearing loss, intellectual disability or another cause
    • you notice: short answers · long pauses · fillers ("well, you know") · restarts · incomplete sentences · vague words ("she") · grammar errors · the listener cannot follow the message
    • risk: boys 2-3:1 · twins · highly heritable (20-40% where there is a family history)
    • prognosis: receptive problems fare worse · school-entry vocabulary predicts school success · oral language predicts reading and writing · secondary social, emotional and behaviour problems are often misread as the cause
    • 40% of Canadian children aged 7-14 with psychiatric disorders have a language impairment
  • Acquired language disorder (aphasia) after stroke, brain injury, tumour, infection, dementia - at least 30% of stroke patients

rows: Knows what to say but cannot get it out in speech or writing
Hears or sees the words but cannot make sense of them
Cannot find the right word for objects, places, events
Cannot use, understand, read or write language

blocks.html: 4. Speech sound disorders

• Sounds develop gradually · by 3 years every child should be 90% intelligible, even to strangers
  • Articulation disorder: trouble making particular sounds (e.g. a lisp) · phonological disorder: patterns of substituting, dropping, adding or changing sounds ("dis" for "this", "do" for "dog")
  • Speech sound disorder (DSM-5): persistent difficulty that hurts intelligibility · early onset · not from cerebral palsy, cleft palate, hearing loss or brain injury (genetic syndromes such as Down syndrome are not excluded)

rows: The brain cannot plan and coordinate the movements · no weakness
Weak, slow, uncoordinated or numb speech muscles · abnormal muscle tone
Little cooing or babbling · late first words · few sounds · trouble combining sounds · may look like an expressive language problem · often with aphasia when acquired
Asymmetric face · drooling, eating difficulty · neurological conditions (stroke, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinson's when acquired)

blocks.html: • Acquired speech disorders: structural (damage or removal of larynx, tongue, jaw) · motor (dysarthria, apraxia)
5. Voice, fluency and social communication

• Voice disorder = a voice that draws attention to itself (pitch, loudness, quality, resonance)
    • causes: misuse · disease · congenital defects · laryngeal trauma or surgery · ageing · neurological (cerebral palsy, spasmodic dysphonia)
    • laryngeal: rough, harsh, hoarse, breathy · resonance: hypernasal (too much nasal air - cleft) vs hyponasal (too little - e.g. deviated septum)
  • Stuttering (childhood-onset fluency disorder): repetitions, prolongations, blocks, broken words, word substitutions
    • normal dysfluency: girls 2-3 years, boys 3-4 years · most outgrow it (65-85% recover)
    • persistence is more likely with: family history · dysfluency over 6 months · other speech or language problems · the child or parent is worried
    • early on: do not react, interrupt or finish their sentences · listen to the content · treat if it persists, the child is bothered, or secondary behaviours appear (facial grimacing) · treatment is behavioural
  • Social (pragmatic) communication disorder: trouble using language socially - greetings, matching the listener, turn-taking, reading what is not said · autism must be ruled out first · becomes clearer in the school years
  • Speech-language pathologists also handle swallowing: arching during feeds · feeds over 30 minutes · coughing or gagging · recurrent pneumonia · poor weight gain
6. Workup and referral

flowchart TD A["Red flag: missed milestone · parent concern
school or behaviour problems · hard to understand"] --> B["HEARING ASSESSMENT first
conductive or sensorineural loss?"] B --> C{"Language or speech?"} C -->|"Language - vocabulary, sentences, understanding"| D["Language disorder
look for autism, intellectual disability, ADHD"] C -->|"Speech - sounds, fluency, voice"| E["Speech sound, fluency or voice disorder"] D --> F{"Preschool or school age?"} E --> F F -->|Preschool| G["Ontario Preschool Speech and Language Program
e.g. tykeTALK"] F -->|"School age"| H["Referral within the school board
or private speech-language pathologist"]

blocks.html:
• Also: neurological and medical exam · screen for comorbidities - ADHD, learning disabilities, autism, brain injury, seizures, genetic syndromes
  • Speech-language pathologists (master's-trained, regulated) assess and treat articulation, language, fluency, voice, swallowing, social communication and literacy · audiologists handle hearing

lectures.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder & Intellectual Disabilities
lectures.title: Autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Every child with global developmental delay or intellectual disability (and autism with dysmorphic features or ID) gets a chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing - not a karyotype. Autism = all 3 social-communication deficits + 2 of 4 restricted, repetitive behaviours, from early development. Intellectual disability = IQ under about 70 plus adaptive deficits, onset in development; global developmental delay is the under-5 label. No drug treats the core of either; aggression is the main reason to medicate, usually with an antipsychotic. Vaccines do not cause autism.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Autism is a disorder of social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviour; intellectual disability is low intelligence plus low adaptive function. They often coexist, share a genetic workup, and are managed the same way - no drug treats the core, so medication targets the problem behaviours.
1. Autism spectrum disorder - diagnosis

• One umbrella diagnosis in DSM-5, replacing autism, Asperger syndrome, childhood disintegrative disorder and pervasive developmental disorder
  • A. Social communication and interaction - all 3
    • social-emotional reciprocity (no back-and-forth conversation, little sharing of interests or emotion)
    • nonverbal communication (eye contact, gestures, facial expression)
    • relationships (adjusting to context, imaginative play, interest in peers)
  • B. Restricted, repetitive behaviour - at least 2 of 4
    • stereotyped movements, object use or speech (hand-flapping, lining up toys, echolalia)
    • insistence on sameness (distress at small changes, rigid routines)
    • fixated interests abnormal in intensity or focus
    • over- or under-reaction to sensory input (indifferent to pain, upset by sounds or textures)
  • C. Present in early development (may only show when social demands exceed capacity, or be masked later) · D. Impairment · E. Not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay
    • both can be diagnosed together when social communication is below the child's general developmental level
2. Autism - who, why, and the workup

• About 1.7% of 8-year-olds · boys about 4.5:1 · rising, mostly from broader criteria and awareness
  • Comorbidities: intellectual disability about a third (31% upper-year notes, 33% medwiki) · seizures 20% (early childhood or adolescence; more with fragile X, tuberous sclerosis)
  • Causes
    • neurodevelopmental - abnormal brain development, not degeneration · larger head circumference (up to 20% above the 97th percentile) and brain size, mostly white matter
    • genetic: 10-15% have copy-number changes · sibling recurrence 5-10%
    • leading psychological theory: missing "theory of mind" (inferring what others think and feel)
    • no link with vaccines
  • Assessment: developmental history from parents · reports from school or daycare · direct observation · speech-language and cognitive assessment · genetic testing with a chromosomal microarray (especially with dysmorphic features or intellectual disability)
    • tools: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (screen) · Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (gold standard, expensive)
  • Differential: hearing impairment · intellectual disability · severe language disorder · social communication disorder · ADHD (attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder) · social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder · Rett syndrome
3. Intellectual disability - diagnosis

• Intellectual deficits, confirmed by clinical assessment and standardized testing: reasoning · problem solving · planning · abstract thinking · judgement · academic learning · learning from experience
    • IQ about 2 standard deviations below the mean - under about 70
  • Adaptive deficits that limit independence and social responsibility: communication · social participation · independent living (self-care, school, work)
  • Onset in the developmental period · severity: mild · moderate · severe · profound

rows: Criteria met on testing - use it whenever the criteria are met

Delay of 2+ standard deviations in 2 or more domains (motor · speech and language · cognition · social · daily living) and cannot yet be tested reliably · reassess later - most go on to intellectual disability
Cannot be graded because of blindness, prelingual deafness, physical disability, severe behaviour or another disorder · reassess later

blocks.html:
• About 1% of the population · boys 1.25:1 · higher with lower maternal education and income
  • Comorbidities: hearing loss 10% · seizures (sources differ: a third of severe and 5-15% of mild in the upper-year notes, about 10% of mild in the medwiki note - check the slides) · cerebral palsy in 30-60% of severe · psychiatric disorders far more common but under-diagnosed
4. Intellectual disability - causes and workup
• The more severe, the more likely a cause is found: about 75% of severe vs under 50% of mild

rows: Fragile X - most common genetic cause · Down syndrome · Rett syndrome
Teratogens: valproate, phenytoin · alcohol · radiation · infections: rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, HIV · inborn errors of metabolism · brain malformations · placental disease
Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy · meningitis, encephalitis · brain injury · infantile spasms · severe deprivation · lead or mercury poisoning

blocks.html:
• First-line genetic tests: chromosomal microarray + fragile X testing in every child with global developmental delay or intellectual disability - not a karyotype
  • Fragile X: CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene · features: long face, large ears, flat feet, lax joints, low tone · ADHD, autism, social anxiety, aggression · premutation carriers can later get a tremor-ataxia syndrome or early ovarian failure

blocks.cap: Workup of global developmental delay or intellectual disability: history, exam, hearing and vision first, then microarray and fragile X, then brain MRI and genetics or metabolic referral, with periodic reassessment

blocks.html: 5. Management

• No medication treats autism or intellectual disability itself - medication only adds to behavioural, educational and speech therapy, aimed at behaviours that disrupt daily life
  • Non-drug, the core: education · speech-language therapy · occupational therapy · social skills training · early intensive behavioural intervention (applied behaviour analysis, at least 20 hours a week, for years) to shift the developmental trajectory while the brain is plastic - helps some children with autism
  • Problem behaviours: look for the cause first - biomedical (pain, seizures, drug side effects) · psychiatric (depression, psychosis, anxiety) · sensory overload (noise, crowds) · communication limits · environment (changes, losses) · past trauma

rows: Aggression (self, others, property) - the commonest reason to start a drug
Frustration, poor emotion regulation and impulse control
Antipsychotics · anticonvulsants or lithium · stimulants or atomoxetine
Stimulants (less effective than in ADHD alone) · atomoxetine · antipsychotics

blocks.html:
• ⚠ Not recommended - no evidence: cannabidiol · antifungals · homeopathic or naturopathic remedies · chelation · special diets (gluten-free)
  • Involve community supports and the family throughout

lectures.name: Disruptive Behavior Disorders
lectures.title: Disruptive behaviour disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ ODD = 6+ months of angry, defiant, vindictive behaviour (4 of 8) without violating others' rights; conduct disorder = 3 of 15 rights-violating behaviours in 12 months. Childhood-onset conduct disorder (before 10) has the worst prognosis and often leads to antisocial personality after 18. ODD severity counts settings: 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3+ severe. First line is structured psychosocial treatment with the parents; multisystemic therapy for conduct disorder. No drug for the disorder itself - treat comorbid ADHD, and risperidone for aggression.

Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) defies and argues; conduct disorder (CD) violates the rights of others. Both are multifactorial, start early, overlap with ADHD (attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder), and are treated with structured psychosocial programmes that involve the parents - not medication.
1. Causes - risk factors in four domains

rows: Family history of behaviour, substance use or mood disorders (genetic coefficient 0.5) · low birth weight · pregnancy and birth complications · brain injury or disease · male sex · autonomic under-reactivity (little anxiety about consequences) · underactive inhibitory regions (frontal lobe, amygdala, hippocampus)

Difficult temperament (fussy, hard to soothe) · low IQ · language and reading problems · inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity · aggression · reads threat into social situations · chronic illness or disability

Parental antisocial behaviour or substance use · domestic violence · separation, single parent · maternal depression · maltreatment, neglect · poor supervision · harsh, coercive or inconsistent discipline
Low income · delinquent peers · disadvantaged, high-crime neighbourhood · being bullied · peer rejection

blocks.html: • The most common reason for youth mental health referral (about 30%) · raise the risk of later psychiatric, social and legal problems
2. Oppositional defiant disorder

• A pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behaviour, or vindictiveness for 6+ months - 4 or more of 8, with at least one person who is not a sibling
    • angry, irritable: loses temper · touchy, easily annoyed · angry and resentful
    • argumentative, defiant: argues with authority · refuses rules or requests · deliberately annoys · blames others
    • vindictive: spiteful at least twice in 6 months
  • Usually feels justified · no major violation of society's rules
  • Frequency: under 5 years → most days · 5 and over → at least weekly · must exceed what is normal for age, sex and culture
  • Not only during psychosis, substance use, depression or bipolar disorder · disruptive mood dysregulation disorder excluded · over 18, antisocial personality disorder excluded
  • Severity by number of settings: mild 1 · moderate 2 · severe 3+
  • Epidemiology: about 3.3% · boys 1.4:1 before adolescence, equal after · starts around 6-8 (preschool symptoms) · about 30% progress to conduct disorder, especially the vindictive and argumentative
3. Conduct disorder
• A persistent pattern that violates others' basic rights or major age-appropriate rules: 3 or more of 15 in 12 months, at least 1 in the last 6 months, with impairment

rows: Bullies, threatens · starts fights · uses a weapon · cruel to people · cruel to animals · steals while confronting a victim · forced sexual activity
Deliberate fire-setting to cause damage · other deliberate destruction
Breaks into a house, building or car · lies to "con" others · shoplifting or forgery
Out at night against parents' rules before 13 · runs away overnight (2+ times, or once for long) · truant before 13

blocks.html:
• Onset specifier: childhood onset (before 10) - worse prognosis, more ADHD, aggression and family dysfunction · adolescent onset (after 10) · unspecified
  • With limited prosocial emotions: 2+ over 12 months - no remorse or guilt · callous, no empathy · unconcerned about performance · shallow affect
  • Severity mild · moderate · severe · not diagnosed when the behaviour is needed to survive (war, extreme poverty)
  • Over 18: diagnose antisocial personality disorder instead if its criteria are met
  • Epidemiology: 2-10%, median 4% · boys 3-5:1 · progression to antisocial personality (sources differ: 30-50% in the upper-year notes, about 40% in the medwiki note - check the slides)
4. Telling them apart

rows: ODD has no aggression to people or animals, destruction or theft, but does include irritable mood · can coexist
Impulsive, but does not violate others' rights or society's rules · can coexist
Same chronic negative mood and outbursts, but more severe
Impulsive aggression not aimed at a goal
Conduct problems that begin with a clear stressor
Does not follow directions because it does not understand them
Defiance driven by fear of being judged

blocks.html: 5. Comorbidities

• ODD: ADHD in about 50%, often seen first
  • CD: up to 90% of early-onset CD had ODD · ADHD 40-70% · depression up to 40% · anxiety 30% · learning disabilities up to 20% · substance use · intellectual disability
  • Consequences: incarceration · school dropout · teen pregnancy · family stress
6. Treatment

• Principles: individualized (causes vary) · earlier is better · structured psychosocial intervention is first line · involve the parents
  • Parent training: Triple P (positive parenting - relationships, attitude, conduct) · parent-child interaction therapy (parent coached in real time) · collaborative problem solving (for ODD - flexibility and cooperation)
  • Functional family therapy: tackles negative attributions, builds positive time together
  • Individual therapy - works better in teens: CBT for social-thinking deficits · social skills · problem solving
  • School: assess and address learning and communication problems · peer promotion of good behaviour · token economy
  • Multisystemic therapy - for conduct disorder, the most effective when given at the right intensity and duration: intensive, over years, across parent, school, vocational, community and justice settings
  • Severe cases: therapeutic residential care, group home or foster care · short hospital stay for severe aggression
  • Medication: none is indicated for ODD or CD themselves
    • treat comorbid conditions - treating ADHD reduces ODD and CD symptoms · treating depression or anxiety reduces outbursts
    • for aggression: risperidone (the most evidence) or other antipsychotics · clonidine
  • Refer to allied professionals where the problems lie - learning and communication assessment, family therapy, school supports
  • Prevention: parent support, education, advocacy, social determinants of health

weeks.label: Week 19 - Psychotic Disorders, Eating Disorders & Mental Health Law

lectures.name: Eating Disorders
lectures.title: Eating disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anorexia = restriction to a significantly low weight; bulimia = binges plus compensation; binge-eating disorder = binges with no compensation. ARFID restricts without any body-image concern. Russell's sign, enlarged salivary glands and enamel erosion point to purging. Daytime heart rate under 50 is one admission criterion on its own. Refeeding syndrome's hallmark is low phosphate - refeed slowly and check electrolytes often. Family-based treatment is first line in adolescents; fluoxetine has evidence in bulimia.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Three questions sort the main eating disorders: is the weight significantly low, are there binges, and is there compensating (purging, fasting, exercise) afterwards? The second question for every patient is whether the body is safe enough to treat at home.
1. What an eating disorder is

• Definition: a persistent disturbance of eating or eating-related behaviour that changes how food is taken in or absorbed, and significantly harms physical health or psychosocial functioning
  • When to be concerned: troubling weight-control behaviours · preoccupation with body, weight and food · fast weight loss · failure to meet expected growth or weight gain · distress from eating behaviours
  • Risk factors
    • family history (higher in identical twins and first-degree relatives) · perfectionist, rigid or impulsive traits · picky eating in childhood
    • at-risk activities: sports with weight classes or a focus on looks (ballet, gymnastics, wrestling, diving, running, modelling)
    • societal body ideals and dieting · abuse and post-traumatic stress disorder (bulimia)
2. Assessment

• Standard psychiatric assessment, plus insight and goals, then:
    • Intake: restriction, rules, fasting, calorie counting, binge eating, sensory- or fear-based avoidance · Output: exercise, vomiting, laxatives, weight-loss substances
    • Drivers: body image · fear of choking or vomiting · History: highest and lowest weight, puberty · review of systems for malnutrition · peers, online, at-risk activities, family food culture
    • Collateral from parents: what they have seen · stressors · whether they can carry out treatment at home
  • Investigations: complete blood count · electrolytes · glucose · creatinine · liver tests · thyroid-stimulating hormone · ECG
  • Differential: depression · anxiety · irritable bowel syndrome · food insecurity · intellectual disability · neglect · medical conditions affecting intake or metabolism
3. Anorexia vs bulimia vs binge-eating disorder

rows: Restricted intake → significantly low weight for age, sex and growth · intense fear of gaining weight (or behaviour that blocks gain) · distorted body experience, self-worth tied to shape, or not seeing how serious the low weight is

Binge = clearly more food than most would eat in a set period (about 2 hours) with loss of control · compensation: vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, exercise · both at least weekly for 3 months · self-worth unduly tied to shape and weight · not only during anorexia

Binges at least weekly for 3 months, with 3 or more of: eating fast · until uncomfortably full · when not hungry · alone from embarrassment · disgust or guilt after · marked distress · no regular compensation

Restricting vs binge-eating/purging type (past 3 months) · severity by body mass index (BMI): mild 17+ · moderate 16-16.99 · severe 15-15.99 · extreme under 15 · youth: BMI percentile or ideal body weight
Severity by compensations per week: mild 1-3 · moderate 4-7 · severe 8-13 · extreme 14+
Severity by binges per week, same cut-offs
1-2% of females · female to male 10:1 · onset 14-18
1-1.5% · 10:1 · slightly older onset (14-22), with dieting and stress · 10-15% move to anorexia
Least sex skew · onset late teens to early adulthood · 5-30% of adults with obesity

Small portions, skipped meals, cutting food up · exercise · cold intolerance · constipation · amenorrhea · hair loss, lanugo · slow heart rate, low blood pressure · osteopenia · arrested growth or puberty
Russell's sign (knuckle calluses) · enlarged salivary glands · dental enamel erosion · Mallory-Weiss tears · electrolyte disturbance · raised serum amylase

Level of care → medical stabilization → nutritional rehabilitation → family-based treatment (gold standard in adolescents) · medication only for comorbidity (SSRI, short-term benzodiazepine, olanzapine for distressing eating-disorder thoughts)
Structured eating (3 meals, 3 snacks) · enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-E), family-based treatment, interpersonal therapy · fluoxetine · topiramate
CBT (also guided self-help), interpersonal therapy, dialectical behaviour therapy · topiramate · lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse)

50% remit with treatment · psychiatric comorbidity 88% · mortality 3.9%

• Anorexia mortality (sources differ: upper-year notes give 5-7%, the medwiki note 5-10% and 10% - check the slides)
  • The medwiki note rates CBT's support as weak for anorexia and bulimia, while the upper-year notes make enhanced CBT the core therapy for bulimia (sources differ - check the slides)

blocks.html: 4. Other feeding and eating disorders

• Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID): avoids food from lack of interest, its sensory features, or fear of choking or vomiting → weight loss or faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, dependence on tube feeds or supplements, or social impairment
    • no body-image disturbance - the key difference from anorexia · more than picky eating
    • equal in boys and girls · linked to autism, anxiety, depression, neglect, developmental delay · outcome similar to anorexia
    • treatment: CBT with exposure, family-based treatment, gradual new foods · appetite stimulants · nasogastric tube if needed
  • Other specified feeding or eating disorder (OSFED): does not fit a full set of criteria · one of the most common diagnoses · atypical anorexia · low-frequency bulimia or binge eating · purging disorder · night eating syndrome
  • Pica: eating non-food (ice, clay, paper, hair) for 1+ month, not developmentally or culturally normal · linked to intellectual disability, autism, pregnancy · rule out iron and zinc deficiency · watch for a bezoar
  • Rumination disorder: repeated regurgitation for 1+ month (re-chewed, re-swallowed or spat out), not from a gut condition · rule out a gastrointestinal cause, treat underlying anxiety
  • Related: orthorexia · relative energy deficiency in sport · muscle dysmorphia · body dysmorphic disorder
5. Medical admission and refeeding

• Admit an adolescent with any of (one is enough):
    • weight: 75% of median BMI for age and sex · arrested growth
    • vital signs: heart rate under 50 by day or under 45 at night · blood pressure under 90/45 · temperature under 35.5 °C · orthostatic change over 20 systolic or 10 diastolic, or pulse rise over 20
    • labs and ECG: dehydration · low potassium, sodium or phosphate · ECG changes such as a long QT
    • behaviour: acute food refusal · uncontrollable bingeing and purging · failed outpatient treatment · family cannot supervise meals
    • complications: syncope, seizure, cardiac arrest, pancreatitis · comorbidity that blocks outpatient care (severe depression, suicidal thoughts, obsessive-compulsive disorder, type 1 diabetes) · concern about refeeding · needs a nasogastric tube

blocks.html:
• Refeeding syndrome: a potentially fatal shift of fluid and electrolytes when a malnourished patient is fed
    • hallmark: low phosphate (hypophosphatemia) · also low potassium, magnesium, calcium, sodium, thiamine, and abnormal glucose
    • why: malnutrition empties the body's phosphate stores while the blood level looks normal · carbohydrate → insulin → cells pull in phosphate, potassium and magnesium → blood levels crash (sources differ: upper-year notes call this a switch from anabolic to catabolic, the medwiki note from catabolic to anabolic - check the slides)
    • results: heart failure · arrhythmia · seizures · delirium · death
    • risk: severe malnutrition and rapid refeeding · 6-27% of hospitalized adolescents
6. Treatment

• Goals: normal eating · restore and keep a healthy weight and growth · stop eating-disorder behaviours · better body image and coping · a healthier relationship between food, body and self
  • Family-based treatment (FBT): parents plan and plate meals at regular times, eaten whether hungry or not (hunger and fullness cues are unreliable in anorexia), then gradually hand control back
    • families are not to blame and are a resource · strong support in anorexia and bulimia
  • CBT: change eating and behaviour · exposure to feared foods · challenge thoughts · bulimia's enhanced CBT is about 20 manualized sessions
  • Others: adolescent-focused therapy · dialectical behaviour therapy · interpersonal therapy · motivational interviewing
  • No medication is best for eating disorders; most treat comorbid anxiety or depression

lectures.name: The Child Welfare System
lectures.title: The child welfare system
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Every suspected abuse or neglect of a child must be reported to CAS: the duty overrides confidentiality, a good-faith report cannot be sued, and only 16-17 year olds are exempt. CAS shares little and owes you no report back. CAS cannot consent to treatment until a court places the child in its care. Admission medical within 72 hours, dental within 7 days. A capable child consents for themselves; surgery needs the caseworker's supervisor. Indigenous placement order: extended family → community → another Indigenous family; the band gets 60 days to plan before adoption.

The lecture follows children through five cases, and each turns on the same three questions: what must the physician report, who is allowed to know, and who can consent to treatment? The Children's Aid Society (CAS) is the agency at the centre of all of them.
1. The Children's Aid Society and its terms

• CAS: investigates abuse, neglect and maltreatment of children aged 0-18, and serious acting-out under age 12 · mandate from Ontario's Child, Youth and Family Services Act (2017) · about 50 non-profit branches in Ontario
  • Kinship care: the child lives with another member of the biological family when the parents cannot cope (under an order of supervision or a temporary care agreement)
  • Temporary care and custody order: the child is in CAS care for a set time · Long-term care: in care beyond that order, ideally with one foster family for the whole stay
  • Crown (society) ward: CAS holds long-term guardianship
  • Capable (the Health Care Consent Act definition): able to understand the information about a treatment and appreciate the foreseeable consequences of deciding or not deciding
2. Reporting and information (Case 1)

• Every suspected case of child abuse or neglect must be reported to CAS - a professional and legal duty that overrides confidentiality and any other law against disclosure
    • a report made in good faith (not maliciously or without reasonable cause) is immune from civil action
    • failing to report: criminal prosecution, civil liability, or professional misconduct (College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario) · Ontario fine up to $5,000 (across Canada $500-$10,000 and up to 1 year in jail)
    • ages 16 and 17: reporting is not mandatory, though they can choose to receive services
  • What CAS tells the physician: only relevant medical details and the general reason the child is followed · few details early in an investigation · no duty to report back after you raise a concern
  • When CAS can decide about treatment
    • urgent treatment refused by the parents → CAS can apprehend the child through an emergency court hearing
    • non-urgent → CAS can apprehend and authorize a medical examination (an exam is not treatment)
    • until a court places the child in CAS care, CAS is not a substitute decision maker
3. How a child comes into care

blocks.html: 4. The team around the child (Case 2)

• Care needs a multidisciplinary team: physician · caseworker · foster parents · school · biological parents where appropriate
  • Access visits: the court sets how often, whether supervised (by a CAS worker or relative), and where · CAS or the parents can ask the court to change or remove them · a crown ward with a long-term access order is usually not eligible for adoption
  • Individual Education Plan (IEP): written by educators for a child with special learning or developmental needs, naming everyone's role
  • Who comes to appointments: the caseworker and foster parent attend (for information, adherence and feedback) unless the child prefers to be seen alone
    • adolescents are always seen alone for part of the visit
    • a possible abuse victim is seen alone, with a nurse present
5. Medical needs of children in care (Case 3)

• Admission medical within 72 hours of entering care · first dental check within 7 days (usually at the admission medical) · then dental check-ups every 6 months (sources differ: upper-year notes give every 12 months - check the slides)
  • Severe dental caries can be a clue to neglect

• Questionnaires caregivers can fill in: Parents' Evaluation of Developmental Status (development and behaviour, birth to 8) · Conners scale (ADHD and disruptive behaviour) · Child Development Inventory (milestones) · Child Behavior Checklist (behaviour and social skills)
  • Visit schedule
    • every visit: the presenting concern · growth · school, placement and visits · immunizations
    • yearly: medications and allergies · diet · teens' alcohol, tobacco, drugs and sexual activity · full exam and teeth · anticipatory guidance
    • as needed: hearing and vision · development and mental health · screening for sexually transmitted infections, HIV, hepatitis B and C, tuberculosis · contraception counselling · referrals
  • Who pays: CAS (prescriptions, glasses, approved over-the-counter drugs) · the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (yearly exam and eye test) · Healthy Smiles Ontario (dental, low-income, 17 and under) · Assistive Devices Program (part of equipment, CAS pays the rest)

blocks.html: 6. Indigenous children (Case 4)

• Since 1985, the law recognizes the right of Indigenous peoples to provide their own child and family services, respecting culture, tradition and extended family
  • Over-represented: 52.2% of children in foster care are Indigenous, against 7.7% of the child population (2016 Census) · urban agencies struggle to recruit Indigenous foster homes
  • Placement order of priority: ① extended family → ② the child's band or Indigenous community → ③ another Indigenous family · a non-Indigenous home is allowed when none is available, and must respect the child's culture
  • The community's role: copies of assessment reports go to the band or community authority · its representative hears placement recommendations
  • Adoption: written notice to the band or community, which has 60 days to submit its own plan, and CAS must consider it
  • Higher rates than non-Indigenous children: infant mortality · injury · respiratory and infectious disease · suicide and depression · abuse · developmental and learning disorders · fetal alcohol spectrum disorder
7. Breaking the cycle (Case 5)

• Needs of children in care continue into adulthood and the next generation · care ends at 18 ("ages out"), with extended care support to 21 for many · some crown wards return to the parents who neglected them
  • Opportunities: public health programs for young parents (Smart Start for Babies, Nurse-Family Partnership) · Canadian Mental Health Association · community and Ontario services · CAS itself

lectures.name: Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia
lectures.title: Psychotic disorders and schizophrenia
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Duration sorts the schizophrenia spectrum: under 1 month = brief psychotic disorder, 1-6 months = schizophreniform, 6+ months = schizophrenia. Schizoaffective needs 2+ weeks of psychosis without a mood episode; psychosis only during mood episodes = mood disorder with psychotic features. Delusional disorder: delusions for 1+ month, otherwise intact. Schizophrenia's criterion A needs delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech. Detailed visual hallucinations suggest an organic cause. Family history is the strongest risk factor; each relapse costs function.
