blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.
Psychosis is a set of symptoms, not a diagnosis. The disorders that cause it are told apart by how long the psychosis lasts and how it lines up with mood episodes.
1. What psychosis is

• Loss of contact with reality: trouble telling what is real from what is not · many causes besides the psychotic disorders
  • Six domains change:
    • Thinking: trouble concentrating, following conversation, remembering · thoughts jumbled · impaired working memory, attention, verbal and visual learning, reasoning, social cognition · slowed processing speed is the most common change · disrupted salience (cannot pick out what matters from what does not)
    • Perception - hallucinations: false perceptions with no outside stimulus, made by the brain (a person born deaf can still hear voices)
      • auditory, the most common: commenting (narrating) · conversing (voices talking to each other) · commanding (can drive harm)
      • visual: rare, poorly formed shapes, shadows, lights · detailed visual hallucinations → think of an organic cause, pseudohallucination or malingering
      • tactile: "inside out" (bugs under the skin) or "outside in" (being touched) · smell and taste: less common, usually foul
    • Beliefs - delusions: fixed, false beliefs from a wrong inference about reality, out of keeping with the person's intelligence and culture, not correctable by reasoning
      • types: persecutory · grandiose · somatic · religious · erotomanic · infidelity · reference · thought broadcasting, insertion, withdrawal
    • Mood: swings, excitement, depression, anxiety, or very little emotion
    • Behaviour: acting differently, often driven by hallucinations and delusions
    • Insight: lacking in 50-70%, completely ("nothing is wrong") or partly ("it's just stress") · a neurological symptom like anosognosia, not tied to intelligence · poor insight → poor adherence
2. Positive vs negative symptoms

rows: Something added that people do not normally experience
Delusions · hallucinations · disorganized thinking · excitement, agitation
Flat affect · alogia (less speech) · avolition (cannot start goal-directed activity) · anergia · anhedonia · asociality · inattention
Negative symptoms → worse outcome, harder to treat

blocks.html: 3. Telling the psychotic disorders apart

rows: Sudden psychotic symptoms (sources differ: the medwiki note lists 2 of schizophrenia's core symptoms, upper-year notes 1 or more - check the slides)
Full return to baseline · often after a marked stressor · can start in pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum
Called "provisional" before recovery · almost all go on to schizophrenia
6+ months, with at least 1 month of core symptoms
Mood episodes, if any, only for a minority of the illness
Major mood episode at the same time as core symptoms, mood present for most of the illness
Psychosis for 2+ weeks with no mood episode · bipolar or depressive type
1+ delusion, hallucinations minor and tied to its theme
Core criteria never met · function and behaviour not markedly odd apart from the delusion · resists medication alone
Hallucinations and/or delusions during or soon after intoxication or withdrawal
Delirium excluded · alcohol, cannabis, phencyclidine, amphetamines, cocaine, hallucinogens, inhalants, sedatives · medications: steroids, interferon, mefloquine, diphenhydramine

blocks.cap: Schizoaffective disorder: psychosis runs alongside the mood episodes and also persists at baseline between them

blocks.html: 4. Schizophrenia

• DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, 5th edition) criteria
    • A: 2+ of delusions · hallucinations · disorganized speech · grossly disorganized or catatonic behaviour · negative symptoms - for a significant part of 1 month (less if treated), and at least one must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech
    • B: work, relationships or self-care well below the previous level (or failure to reach the expected level in a young person)
    • C: 6 months of continuous signs, including 1 month of criterion A (the rest may be prodromal or residual symptoms)
    • D-F: not schizoaffective or a mood disorder · not from a substance or medical condition · with past autism or a communication disorder, needs prominent delusions or hallucinations for 1 month
  • Epidemiology: lifetime risk about 1% (any psychotic disorder about 3%) · same incidence worldwide, regardless of culture, class or background · men and women equally · first episode usually 18-24 (a second, late peak in women around 50-54) · 5-13% die by suicide
  • Risk factors
    • family history is the strongest (about 80% heritable): sibling 8% · one parent 12% · two parents 40% · non-identical twin 12% · identical twin 47%
    • cannabis in early adolescence (12-18; higher-THC products carry more risk; use after 25 adds no risk) · birth complications · older father · childhood trauma, refugee migration · DiGeorge syndrome (25%)
  • Course: brain changes are present near birth, but symptoms appear in late adolescence as the brain finishes pruning · premorbid → prodrome → active illness → chronic or residual phase
    • each relapse leaves a less complete recovery, so engaging early after the first episode matters most

blocks.cap: Each relapse after the first episode lowers the level of functioning regained, with progressive brain tissue loss and eventual treatment resistance

rows: Mood symptoms, or family history of mood disorder
Single, divorced or widowed, poor supports
Negative or cognitive symptoms · neurological signs · brain changes · many relapses

blocks.html: • Relapse risk: stopping medication 4× · ongoing substance use 3× · carers' critical comments 2.3× · poor premorbid adjustment 2.2×
5. Treatment in outline

• Goals: reduce symptoms · maximize quality of life and function · support recovery and life goals
  • Antipsychotics are the gold standard, but medication alone leaves relapse high: add psychoeducation for patient and family, treatment of substance use, CBT and cognitive rehabilitation, case management (housing, school, work), and crisis support
  • Full detail in 04 - Treatment of Psychotic Disorders

lectures.name: Treatment of Psychotic Disorders
lectures.title: Treatment of psychotic disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic and the drug for treatment-resistant psychosis (2 failed trials of 4-6 weeks), but it needs blood monitoring for agranulocytosis. 1st generation = potent dopamine block, positive symptoms only, extrapyramidal effects; 2nd = sedation and weight gain; 3rd = partial agonist. Acute dystonia is an emergency; akathisia gets a beta-blocker; parkinsonism an anticholinergic. All antipsychotics can prolong the QT; risperidone is worst for sexual side effects. Stay on treatment 12-18 months after a first episode. Carers' critical comments are the 3rd biggest relapse risk.

Antipsychotics treat psychosis by blocking dopamine; the three generations differ in how hard they block it, and that sets their side effects. Part 2 of the lecture is the reminder that medication is only one component: the psychosocial supports decide relapse.
1. Dopamine and psychosis

rows: How we feel about what we notice, and remembering it
Overactive → faulty salience, false connections, hallucinations → positive symptoms
Learning, memory, motivation, organizing behaviour (highly developed in humans)

blocks.html:
• Glutamate (NMDA receptors) and serotonin are involved too, but nothing yet treats them · the most effective antipsychotic, clozapine, is one of the least dopamine-blocking
  • About 60% receptor blockade is enough · more is not better: stiffness, tremor, fatigue, sexual effects (upper-year notes)

blocks.alt: dopamine pathways in psychosis - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The four dopamine pathways: mesolimbic overactivity gives positive symptoms, mesocortical underactivity negative symptoms; nigrostriatal controls movement, tuberoinfundibular prolactin

blocks.html: 2. Typical vs atypical antipsychotics

rows: Lower dopamine affinity relative to serotonin and histamine receptors
Dopamine antagonist and partial agonist - balances dopamine rather than blocking it
risperidone · quetiapine · olanzapine · ziprasidone · paliperidone · clozapine
Designed to help negative symptoms too, but no more effective than 1st generation
Designed for fewer side effects · not everyone responds
Extrapyramidal · sexual · low blood pressure · cognitive dulling
Sedation · weight gain → metabolic syndrome (worst with clozapine and olanzapine)
Restlessness · nausea · some weight gain · sexual
Emergency department · patients who cannot take or do not respond to newer drugs
Widely used, also for sleep, bipolar disorder, add-on in depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder, severe ADHD, autism, dementia-related aggression - use judiciously given the metabolic risk

blocks.html:
• On 2nd generation drugs: routine metabolic bloodwork every 6 months
  • In a first episode, 1st and 2nd generation drugs work equally well
3. Clozapine

• The most effective antipsychotic · the drug for treatment-resistant psychosis = 2 or more antipsychotics tried for 4-6 weeks each · works in about 2 of 3 such cases
  • Very low potency, acts on dozens of receptors including serotonin
  • Side effects: weight gain · sedation · fast heart rate · seizures · arrhythmia · rare but serious agranulocytosis (a rapid fall in white blood cells), so it needs blood monitoring
4. Side effects and their treatment

rows: Sudden painful spasm: oculogyric crisis (eyes roll up) · blepharospasm · torticollis · trismus (jaw) · opisthotonus (back arches) · laryngospasm
An emergency: lower the dose + diphenhydramine, a benzodiazepine or an anticholinergic
Tremor · rigidity · slow movement · postural instability
Severe inner and physical restlessness · very distressing, linked to suicide
Involuntary movements of face, lips, tongue, jaw, limbs, head
Fast heart rate · low blood pressure · QT prolongation → torsades de pointes
Amenorrhea, cycle changes, breast enlargement or gynecomastia · erectile and ejaculation problems · low libido
All, especially risperidone · less prolactin effect with 3rd generation

blocks.html: 5. Using antipsychotics

• Onset: sleep and agitation improve in hours to days · a good response in about 2 weeks · full remission 4-8 weeks (sources differ: upper-year notes also give 2-3 weeks for the antipsychotic effect and 6-12 weeks for the maximum - check the slides)
  • Start low, go slow
  • Long-acting injectables (paliperidone, aripiprazole) help adherence - a few missed doses raise relapse risk
  • After a first episode, continue for at least 12-18 months · relapse is highest in the first 2 years · most need a lower maintenance dose long term · no way to predict who can stop
6. Psychosocial treatment

• Aims: psychoeducation and normalizing · less distress · skills for stress and recovery · build on strengths and values · empowerment · a meaningful life
  • Expressed emotion (carers' hostility, criticism or over-involvement) is the 3rd biggest relapse risk, after stopping medication and drug use
  • Components
    • case management: the first point of contact · coordinates housing, income, school, work, court and family · psychoeducation and support
    • patient psychoeducation (informal, group, written) · family psychoeducation early and often - reduces relapse
    • skills: social, daily living, study, stress and symptom management · employment support · cognitive remediation (working memory, processing speed)
    • CBT in prodrome, active illness and recovery, at least 12-16 sessions
    • Assertive community treatment (ACT): a mobile team with frequent contact and outreach (into shelters) for people with major barriers - homelessness, severe substance use
    • early intervention programs: less relapse and readmission · fewer positive and negative symptoms · better function · less substance use · suicide rate halved
  • Prevention: detect childhood trauma and neglect · support at-risk groups (refugee migration) · prevent early substance use
7. Stigma

• Predicts poorer functioning, more positive symptoms, poorer recovery, depression, shame and low self-esteem
  • People with schizophrenia are far more often victims of violence than perpetrators · half of violence that does occur is in the first, untreated episode
  • How clinicians add to stigma: labelling ("you are schizophrenic" vs "you are experiencing psychosis") · hopeless messages · invalidating ("that's just your psychosis") · ignoring the fear psychosis causes · dismissive body language · assuming danger · neglecting other health needs
  • LEAP for a patient with poor insight: Learn · Empathize · Agree · Partner

lectures.name: Consent, Capacity, and the Mental Health Act
lectures.title: Consent, capacity and the Mental Health Act
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Form 1 = any physician who saw the patient in the past 7 days, holds 72 hours for assessment; Form 3 = a different physician, involuntary admission for 14 days. Form 2 comes from a justice of the peace; Form 4 renews for a month and may be the same physician. Box B (deterioration) needs prior response to treatment, incapacity and SDM consent. Capacity = understand + appreciate. Duty to warn: identifiable person, serious harm, imminent - permitted, not required. A known prior capable wish beats both the SDM and an emergency.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Two Ontario laws answer two different questions. The Mental Health Act (MHA) decides whether a person can be held for psychiatric assessment or admission against their will; the Health Care Consent Act (HCCA) decides who agrees to treatment - for every kind of treatment, not just psychiatric.
1. Involuntary admission: the forms

rows: Any physician who has examined the person in the past 7 days
Allows the person to be held for a psychiatric assessment - not an admission, so the bar is relatively low
Must be acted on within 7 days · holds for up to 72 hours
Tells the patient they are on a Form 1 and why
Original to the patient, copy in the chart
A justice of the peace, on information from anyone (often family)
Police bring the person in for assessment (apprehension, not detention)
A different physician from the Form 1 (usually a psychiatrist)
Notice of the right to rights advice
Can be the same physician as the Form 3
A physician, agreed to by the patient or substitute decision maker
Treatment in the community instead of hospital
6 months, renewable · for 2+ admissions or 30+ days in hospital in the past 3 years

blocks.html:
• Don't let a form expire: if it lapses before the next one, and the patient was not expressly told they are now voluntary, you are back to a Form 1
  • Rights: a Form 3 or 4 automatically brings a rights advisor to meet the patient privately · the patient can contest, with a hearing within 3-5 business days
  • If a family member has been through the hard process of getting a Form 2, at least refer to psychiatry
2. Form 1 criteria: Box A and Box B
• Every Form 1 needs a mental disorder (very broad: any disease or disability of the mind) plus risk, in a person who will not or cannot be a voluntary patient · only one box needs to be met

rows: Has threatened or attempted self-harm · has been violent or made others fear harm · has shown a lack of competence to care for self

All of: previously treated for a recurring mental disorder · improved with that treatment · now has the same or a similar disorder · incapable of consenting and the substitute decision maker has consented
Likely and imminent serious bodily harm to self · to others · or serious physical impairment
Likely serious harm to self or others, or substantial mental or physical deterioration
Planning suicide (writing a note, rehoming pets) · command hallucinations to harm · catatonic depression, not eating or drinking
Added in 2000 · not useful in a first episode or an emergency · police cannot use it

blocks.html: • The medwiki note labels the two parts a "past/present test" and a "future test" but maps them the other way round (sources differ - check the slides)
3. Breaking confidentiality: the duty to warn

• A permission, not an obligation, endorsed by the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Medical Protective Association and the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario
  • All three must hold:
    • ① a clear risk to an identifiable person or group
    • ② a risk of serious bodily harm or death
    • ③ the danger is imminent
4. Consent to treatment (Health Care Consent Act)

• Applies to all treatment (even physiotherapy) · valid consent is ① voluntary ② informed ③ capable
  • Voluntary: no deception or coercion
  • Informed: what a reasonable person would want to know - the nature of the treatment · expected benefits · risks, including rare but serious ones · side effects · alternatives · likely result of no treatment · and answers to all questions
  • Capable - the two-part test: the patient must be able to
    • understand the information relevant to the decision, and
    • appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision, or of not deciding
  • Who judges capacity: the clinician proposing the treatment · who consents for an incapable patient: the substitute decision maker (SDM)
5. Substitute decision makers

• Hierarchy: ① guardian → ② attorney for personal care → ③ representative appointed by the Consent and Capacity Board → ④ spouse or partner → ⑤ child or parent → ⑥ sibling → ⑦ other relative → ⑧ Public Guardian and Trustee
    • spouses: married, or living together for 1 year, or parents of a child together, or with a cohabitation agreement
    • siblings who cannot agree → the Public Guardian and Trustee decides
  • To act, an SDM must be: capable for that treatment · 16 or older (unless a parent) · not barred by a court · available · willing
  • How an SDM decides: a known, applicable prior capable wish must be followed · otherwise best interests, the patient's values and beliefs, and any incapable wishes
  • Emergency treatment without consent is allowed when delay would prolong suffering or risk serious bodily harm · note the reasons and find an SDM · an emergency does not override a prior capable wish (e.g. a do-not-resuscitate order)
  • Challenges: the patient can ask the Consent and Capacity Board to review a finding of incapacity or a detention, appeal its ruling to the courts, and challenge the choice of SDM

lectures.name: Substance Use Disorders
lectures.title: Substance use disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Alcohol (and benzodiazepine) withdrawal can kill through seizures and delirium tremens, so it is scored with the CIWA-Ar and treated with benzodiazepines plus IM thiamine; opioid withdrawal is miserable but not fatal. Substance use disorder = 2+ of 11 criteria in 12 months; 6+ is severe. Pinpoint pupils in opioid overdose, dilated pupils in opioid withdrawal and stimulant use. Visual hallucinations in withdrawal point to alcohol. Methadone is a full agonist, buprenorphine a partial one, naloxone an antagonist. Naltrexone and acamprosate for alcohol use disorder; varenicline plus a patch for smoking.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Substance use runs on a spectrum and becomes a disorder at 2 of 11 criteria in a year. Each drug class is then learned the same way - intoxication, withdrawal, treatment - and the question that matters at the bedside is which withdrawals can kill (alcohol and benzodiazepines) and which only feel like they might (opioids).
1. A spectrum, and a reward circuit

• 20% of Canadians aged 15+ have a substance use disorder at some point, most often alcohol or cannabis (upper-year notes: 1 in 15 over age 15, most commonly alcohol - sources differ, check the slides)
  • The spectrum: beneficial → non-problematic → problematic (negative consequences: impaired driving, binges) → chronic dependence (habitual and compulsive despite harm)
  • Neurobiology: dysregulated mesolimbic dopamine - the ventral tegmental area releases dopamine into the nucleus accumbens (reward), which keeps reward-seeking going · the mesocortical pathway is secondary (the transcluded condition note names the mesocortical pathway - check the slides)
2. DSM-5 substance use disorder

• At least 2 of 11 in the past 12 months, in four groups:
    • control: more or longer than intended · cannot cut down · much time spent getting, using, recovering · craving
    • social: failing work, school or home roles · use despite relationship problems · activities given up
    • risk: use when physically hazardous · use despite a known physical or psychological problem
    • pharmacological: tolerance · withdrawal
  • Severity: mild 2-3 · moderate 4-5 · severe 6+ · remission: early after 3 months, sustained after 1 year · "on maintenance therapy"
3. Withdrawal syndromes compared

rows: Slurred speech · poor coordination · unsteady gait · nystagmus · poor attention or memory · stupor, coma

Starts 4-12 h after the last drink: sweating, fast heart rate · tremor · insomnia · nausea, vomiting · agitation · transient hallucinations (visual = red flag) · seizures at 12-48 h · delirium tremens at 48-96 h
Same picture as alcohol (DSM-5 groups them)
No separate detail in the sources
Euphoria, then apathy · pinpoint pupils · drowsiness to coma · slurred speech · toxidrome: coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, low blood pressure, low temperature, low reflexes
Low mood · nausea, vomiting, diarrhea · muscle aches · tears, runny nose · dilated pupils · sweating · yawning · fever · insomnia
Overdose kills; withdrawal is not fatal, but it drives re-use
COWS score · opioid agonist · symptom relief: clonidine, ondansetron, loperamide, NSAIDs
Euphoria, hypervigilance, anxiety, anger · fast or slow heart rate · dilated pupils · high or low blood pressure · sweating · weight loss · chest pain, arrhythmia, seizures · paranoia, psychosis
"Crash": low mood + fatigue · vivid nightmares · too much or too little sleep · increased appetite · slowing or agitation
Overdose: overheating, seizures, kidney injury · injecting raises suicide risk
No medication given in the sources

blocks.html: • Cannabis: withdrawal (sleep problems, irritability, restlessness, appetite loss) has no approved medication, nor does the use disorder · Nicotine: withdrawal handled with nicotine replacement
4. Alcohol

• Drinking guidance: older low-risk guidelines - women 10 a week (2 a day), men 15 a week (3 a day) · Canada's 2023 guidance: 1-2 a week low risk · 3-6 moderate · 7+ high
  • Screening: the AUDIT (10 items, about 97% sensitive and 78% specific) beats CAGE and the single-question screen · AUDIT-C (3 items) measures consumption only
  • Why withdrawal is dangerous: chronic alcohol leaves too little GABA and too much glutamate → a hyperexcitable brain → seizures, plus autonomic overdrive

blocks.cap: Alcohol withdrawal over days: minor withdrawal and hallucinosis peak at 1-2 days, seizures around day 1-2, delirium tremens peaks around day 3-4

blocks.html: • Labs: point-of-care glucose · electrolytes with calcium, magnesium, phosphate · complete blood count · clotting · liver tests · blood alcohol

• The note says thiamine must be intramuscular because oral thiamine is poorly absorbed · thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Agitated intoxication: antipsychotic with breathing monitored, not a benzodiazepine
  • Alcohol use disorder: naltrexone once daily (cuts drinking up to 50%; not with liver dysfunction) · acamprosate three times daily · motivational interviewing · peer support (Alcoholics Anonymous, SMART Recovery) · CBT · family therapy
5. Opioids

• Overdose → naloxone as soon as it is suspected
  • Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS): scores withdrawal and guides buprenorphine induction

rows: Maintenance or taper · high dependence · sedation, respiratory depression, constipation
Reverses overdose · triggers withdrawal in a dependent person

blocks.html: • Harm reduction is the gold standard: do not use alone · carry a naloxone kit · safe equipment · supervised use
6. Cannabis, tobacco, stimulants, inhalants

• Cannabis: THC is the main psychoactive compound · use disorder in 1 in 11 users, 1 in 6 who start as teenagers, 25-50% of daily users · raises the risk of psychosis and schizophrenia · cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome: cyclical vomiting relieved by hot showers · urine positive up to a month in chronic users · harm reduction with Canada's Lower-Risk Cannabis Use Guidelines
  • Tobacco: the most used substance in schizophrenia · brief interventions and motivational interviewing fit into any visit · varenicline + nicotine patch = best practice · bupropion + patch beats placebo
  • Stimulants: binge-and-crash pattern · crystal meth is common in London emergency departments · intoxication brings anxiety, panic, paranoia, psychosis, confusion, aggression · harm reduction starting with psychoeducation
  • Inhalants: volatile solvents (glue, gasoline, paint thinner - most common) · aerosols · gases (nitrous oxide, butane) · nitrites ("poppers") · users mostly aged 10-16 · immediate, brief high · chronic use → brain atrophy and nerve damage resembling multiple sclerosis
7. Treating substance use disorders

• Harm reduction and trauma-informed care are the main approach: understand the community · prioritize safety · stigma-free care · advocate for policy
  • Stigma: self (internalized) · social (attitudes, labels, media) · structural (services designed in stigmatizing ways) · people who inject drugs are the most stigmatized
    • swap labels for assessment: "drug-seeking" → assess cravings, withdrawal, pain · "attention-seeking" → trying to connect
    • people with a substance use disorder often need more pain medication for the same effect
  • Stages of change guide the approach · relapse risk: cravings · coping · emotional state · expectations · prevention: warning signs, coping plans, chain analysis, medication, support
  • Interventions: biological (treat comorbid psychiatric disorders + the drugs above) · psychological (motivational interviewing, CBT, community reinforcement, trauma therapy) · social (case management, housing first, needle exchange, peers, safe supply, detox, residential treatment with waits of 1+ year)

lectures.name: Concurrent Mental Health and Substance Use Disorders
lectures.title: Concurrent mental health and substance use disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Treat both disorders together, and match the program to severity: both severe = a concurrent disorders program (quadrant IV). About half of people with a psychotic disorder have a substance use disorder; tobacco is the most used. In anxiety, the anxiety disorder usually comes first; panic links to alcohol, generalized anxiety to illicit drugs. Urine toxicology clarifies, it never punishes. Substance use makes psychosis start earlier, last longer and relapse more.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

A concurrent disorder means the patient meets the full criteria for both a mental disorder and a substance use disorder. Each worsens the other, so both are treated together, in a program chosen by how severe each one is.
1. How common, and why it matters

• Substance use disorders are among the most common comorbidities of severe mental illness
    • about 50% of people with a psychotic disorder have one, against about 15% of the general population
  • Substance use worsens the course of the mental illness and increases hospitalization
2. Assessment and recovery

• Diagnose both: each disorder must meet its own criteria
  • Ask about: patterns of use · cravings and triggers · current coping · how emotional states change use · physical health, including acute or chronic pain · withdrawal symptoms
  • History: substance history (age started, periods of not using) · psychiatric · family · medical · collateral · urine toxicology - to clarify what was taken, never punitive · assessment over time (longitudinal)
  • Recovery = empowerment · self-management · engagement with community and care team · better functioning · a meaningful quality of life
    • ① ask what the patient wants from recovery (e.g. going back to school) · ② expect setbacks, and keep hope and positive expectations
  • VEAR model: Vulnerability → Exposure → Addiction → Recovery, marking the transition points and what to target at each

blocks.cap: VEAR model: vulnerability (genetic, childhood), exposure (adolescent risk factors), addiction (adult brain changes, aggravating and harm-reduction factors), then recovery and its treatments

blocks.html: 3. The three main pairings

rows: Mood disorders + substance use (major depression, persistent depressive disorder, bipolar disorders)
Each raises the risk of the other and changes its course

Map mood changes against substance use · find what explains the overlap, especially mood lability · predisposing factors (genetic, environmental, psychological) · psychoeducation · treat both with an individual plan

About 75% of people with an anxiety disorder use substances · the anxiety disorder usually comes first · 2-5× the risk of a substance use disorder · panic disorder → alcohol · generalized anxiety disorder → illicit drugs
Predisposing factors · how withdrawal feeds anxiety · psychoeducation on substances and anxiety · treat both

Schizophrenia: 5× the risk of a substance use disorder · tobacco is the most used (55-85% have nicotine use disorder), then cannabis · more binge drinking · substances, especially crystal meth, mimic psychosis, sometimes beyond intoxication
Substance use brings on psychosis earlier, makes symptoms more intense and longer, raises relapse and treatment resistance, and lengthens hospital stays

blocks.html: 4. Matching care to severity: the quadrants of care
• Social determinants of health shape whether a patient can succeed in treatment, so consider them for each patient

lectures.name: Sleep Disorders
lectures.title: Sleep disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Insomnia is a clinical diagnosis treated first with CBT for insomnia - a sleep study is not indicated. Obstructive sleep apnea is the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness; CPAP is the treatment. Central apnea has no breathing effort during pauses. Cataplexy (emotion-triggered loss of tone) points to narcolepsy. NREM parasomnias: children, early night, no memory; REM sleep behaviour disorder: older men, late night, dream recalled, a warning sign for Parkinson and Lewy body disease. Restless legs = awake and voluntary, check ferritin; periodic limb movements = asleep and involuntary, needs a study.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Sort the complaint first: can't sleep (insomnia), sleepy by day despite enough time in bed (sleep apnea, narcolepsy), strange behaviour during sleep (parasomnias), or an urge to move the legs at rest (restless legs). Only some of these need a sleep study - insomnia does not.
1. Normal sleep

• Two kinds of sleep: non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, about 75-80% · rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, about 20-25%
    • Stage N1: the transition from waking · 1-7 minutes, 2-5% of sleep · theta waves · easily disrupted
    • Stage N2: most of the night (45-55%) · sleep spindles and K-complexes, linked to memory consolidation · harder to wake
    • Stage N3 (slow-wave sleep): high-voltage slow delta waves · hardest to wake · growth hormone release · daily brain recovery · sympathetic activity falls
    • REM: low-voltage fast "sawtooth" waves · muscle atonia so dreams are not acted out · vivid dreams · easy to wake
  • Cycling: the first NREM-REM cycle is about 90 minutes, later cycles up to 120 · slow-wave sleep is concentrated in the first third of the night, REM in the last third
  • Age: the need for sleep falls with age · REM falls with age · newborns sleep in chunks

blocks.cap: A night of sleep: deep stage 3 sleep early in the night, longer REM periods toward morning

blocks.html: 2. Measuring sleep

• Polysomnography (overnight sleep study): brain waves (EEG) · eye movements · chin and leg muscle activity (tibialis anterior, for leg movements) · airflow and chest and abdominal effort · oxygen saturation · ECG · snoring microphone · body position · rarely video
  • Order it for: obstructive sleep apnea (90-95% of referrals) · narcolepsy · parasomnias
  • Do not order it for insomnia or as a general look at sleep - only to rule out another sleep disorder

blocks.html: 3. Comparing the main sleep disorders

rows: Dissatisfied with sleep amount or quality despite the chance to sleep
Upper airway closes during sleep → oxygen drops and brief arousals
Abnormal behaviour or experiences during sleep
Trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking early · 3 nights a week for 3 months · distress or impairment
Snoring · witnessed apneas · most common cause of excessive daytime sleepiness · morning headache · poor concentration
Sleep lapses 3 times a week for 3 months plus cataplexy, low hypocretin, or short REM latency · tetrad: sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations
NREM type: incomplete waking from deep sleep, first third of night, no memory · REM type: dream enactment, last third, recalls dream
Most common sleep complaint · about 10% meet criteria · comorbid with medical and psychiatric illness
About 20% of the population · linked to resistant hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, coronary disease
NREM: mostly children · REM sleep behaviour disorder: older men
Clinical · sleep diary · actigraphy · sleep study only to rule out others
Sleep study → apnea-hypopnea index: mild 5-14 · moderate 15-29 · severe 30+ · Epworth, STOP-BANG
Sleep study + multiple sleep latency test: mean latency 8 minutes or less, REM at sleep onset
Collateral history from bed partner or parent · video rarely captures events
CBT for insomnia first (as effective as pills, fewer side effects) · cautious hypnotics
CPAP · dental appliance · surgery (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty) · weight loss, less alcohol
Stimulants · modafinil · venlafaxine or other antidepressants for cataplexy and paralysis · sodium oxybate (specialist)
Safety of the sleep environment · avoid sleep deprivation and alcohol · clonazepam or melatonin

blocks.html: 4. Insomnia

• Diagnosis by history: sleep-wake diary · actigraphy (a wrist tracker, not used much) · sleep study only to rule out another disorder
  • Treatment
    • CBT for insomnia is first line - few practitioners
    • Sleep hygiene alone does not work - do not confuse it with the CBT elements that do (fixed wake time, bed only when sleepy, bed only for sleep)
    • Medication: benzodiazepines and "z-drugs" (zolpidem, eszopiclone) with caution - dependence, falls in the elderly · melatonin helps about a third, minor effect · avoid alcohol and cannabis · over-the-counter antihistamines work but cause dependence
    • Sedating antidepressants and antipsychotics: the medwiki note says avoid unless depression is present, the upper-year notes list them as options (sources differ - check the slides)
5. Sleep apnea

• Obstructive: the airway collapses, breathing effort continues until the patient gasps awake
    • CPAP is the treatment of choice - pressure splints the airway open
    • dental appliance (moves the jaw forward) for mild to moderate · surgery for selected patients · weight loss
  • Central sleep apnea: the brain stops signalling to breathe - no breathing effort during the pauses
    • causes: heart failure, stroke, opioids · treat the cause · bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP), as CPAP can worsen it
6. Narcolepsy

• Cause: loss of hypothalamic neurons making hypocretin (orexin), which keeps us awake - injury, autoimmune, infection
  • Cataplexy: sudden loss of muscle tone (knees, face, neck) triggered by strong emotion, lasting seconds
  • Hypnagogic (falling asleep) and hypnopompic (waking) hallucinations · sleep paralysis for seconds to minutes
  • Cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin: the upper-year notes give a cut-off of 100 pg/mL, the medwiki note only says it is deficient (check the slides)
7. Circadian rhythm disorders

• The body clock is out of step with the required schedule → insomnia or daytime sleepiness
  • Delayed sleep phase: sleeps and wakes later than socially acceptable · about 7% of adolescents · longer body-clock period, more sensitivity to evening light
    • treatment: consistent wake time · morning bright light · evening melatonin
  • Advanced sleep phase: sleeps and wakes too early · others: irregular, non-24-hour, shift work
8. Parasomnias

• NREM parasomnias (children, first third of night, no recall): confusional arousals · sleepwalking · sleep terrors (scream, intense fear, inconsolable)
    • triggers: sleep deprivation · stress · alcohol · sedatives including z-drugs · also sleep-related eating and sexual behaviour
    • treatment: reassurance · safe environment (locks, barriers) · regular sleep · clonazepam last
  • Nightmares vs sleep terrors: nightmares come from REM with vivid recall; terrors from NREM with amnesia
  • REM sleep behaviour disorder: loss of REM atonia → punching, kicking out violent dreams, second half of night · wakes quickly and remembers the dream · older men
    • often precedes Parkinson disease or dementia with Lewy bodies
    • treatment: safety · melatonin · clonazepam
9. Restless legs and periodic limb movements

• Restless legs syndrome: an urge to move the legs while awake at rest, worse in the evening, relieved by movement · 3 times a week for 3 months · clinical diagnosis, no sleep study
    • commonest cause: low ferritin (iron deficiency) · also kidney failure, neuropathy, pregnancy, multiple sclerosis · SSRIs and mirtazapine can trigger it
    • treatment: iron until ferritin above 75 · gabapentin or pregabalin · dopamine agonists: the medwiki note lists pramipexole and ropinirole as helpful, the upper-year notes say they can make it worse (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Periodic limb movement disorder: involuntary leg jerks while asleep · in over 80% of restless legs patients · needs a sleep study
10. Sleep myths
• Short and long sleepers both have higher mortality - the right amount is whatever avoids daytime sleepiness · blue light and activity trackers: weak evidence

lectures.name: Somatic Symptom Disorders
lectures.title: Somatic symptom and related disorders
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Unconscious production with no gain = somatic symptom and related disorders; intentional production for the sick role = factitious disorder; intentional for an external reward = malingering. Illness anxiety has few or no symptoms - the fear of disease is the problem. Conversion disorder shows a mismatch with known neurology (Hoover's sign, improvement with distraction). Somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety both need 6+ months. Treatment aims at function and coping, started early, with a multidisciplinary plan.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

The suffering is real whether or not the symptom is medically explained. These disorders are told apart by two questions: is the symptom produced consciously, and what is gained from it? The aim of treatment is coping and function, not cure.
1. The problem of definition

• Medically unexplained symptoms: pain in several places · disturbed function of an organ system · fatigue
    • may be a physiological disturbance, emotion, or a condition not yet diagnosed
    • common: 15-25% in primary care · 39-50% in specialist clinics · over 60% in neurology
  • Many names, depending on who sees the patient: psychogenic, psychosomatic, somatoform, functional, conversion, "hysteria"
  • Functional disorders exist in every system: irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia · fibromyalgia · non-cardiac chest pain · chronic fatigue syndrome · tension headache, functional seizures and movement disorders · temporomandibular joint dysfunction
    • more often female · overlap with anxiety and depression
2. Telling the disorders apart

rows: 1 or more distressing somatic symptoms + excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours about them
Preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness, with no or only mild symptoms
Altered voluntary motor or sensory function incompatible with known disease
Falsifies or induces illness in self or another, with no external reward
Fakes or exaggerates for an external reward (time off work, drugs, avoiding arrest)
At least 1 of: disproportionate thoughts about seriousness · persistently high health anxiety · excessive time and energy on symptoms · symptomatic for 6+ months (the symptom itself may change)
High health anxiety · excessive checking or maladaptive avoidance · 6+ months · the feared illness may change
Clinical findings show the mismatch · not better explained · distress or impairment
Deception evident · presents self (or a victim) as ill or injured
Symptom type (weakness, movement, seizures, sensory, speech, swallowing) · acute (under 6 months) or persistent · with or without stressor
Single or recurrent episodes · imposed on self vs imposed on another (by proxy)
Internal psychological gain (sources differ: upper-year notes say internal gain, the medwiki figure groups it with no gain - check the slides)

blocks.html:
• Other specified: brief somatic symptom or illness anxiety disorder (under 6 months) · pseudocyesis (a false but non-delusional belief in pregnancy, with physical signs)
  • Conversion on exam: symptoms improve with distraction - Hoover's sign (weak hip extension returns with opposite hip flexion against resistance) · tremor entrainment · controlled arm drop in a "seizure"

blocks.alt: comparison of somatic disorders, factitious disorder, and malingering.png
blocks.cap: Sorting unexplained symptoms by how they are produced, why, and for what gain

blocks.html: 3. Causes: many at once

• Genetics: 5-10 times more common in first-degree relatives
  • Stress: corticotropin-releasing hormone and acetylcholine alter gut motility
  • Psychodynamic: an unconscious conflict converted into a body symptom
  • Trauma and abuse · learning (illness behaviour modelled in the family, secondary gain of the sick role)
  • Emotion and communication: limited vocabulary for feelings · culture and family that stigmatize psychological distress
  • Family systems (Minuchin): enmeshment · overprotection · rigidity · no conflict resolution
  • Brain changes: larger left amygdala, striatum, cerebellum, fusiform gyrus and both thalami · smaller left somatosensory cortex
4. Assessment

• Questionnaires: Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15) · Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire · Short-Form General Health Survey
  • Differential: an undiagnosed medical condition · panic disorder (acute episodes) · generalized anxiety (many worries, not only health) · depression · obsessive-compulsive disorder (intrusive thoughts with compulsions) · delusional disorder (belief held with delusional intensity) · body dysmorphic disorder (appearance, not symptoms)
5. Management: holistic and integrated

• Alliance first: take the concerns seriously · realistic, measurable goals · the goal is to manage and cope, not cure
  • Physical: physiotherapy · heat and cold · TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) · acupuncture · massage · injections and nerve blocks
  • Medication, stepwise (WHO pain ladder): non-opioid (NSAIDs, acetaminophen) → weak opioid → strong opioid, ± adjuvants
    • antidepressants (tricyclics, duloxetine, venlafaxine, trazodone) relieve pain independent of mood · anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin) for neuropathic pain and migraine
    • muscle relaxants do not help chronic pain · opioids only after other options fail, with a documented agreement and review of function and aberrant use at every visit
  • Psychological: CBT · interpersonal therapy · hypnosis · biofeedback · EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) · acceptance and commitment therapy · mindfulness · expressive writing · family therapy
  • Rehabilitation: education · pacing · ergonomics · exercise (aerobic, strengthening, stretching; yoga and tai chi)
  • Secondary prevention: intervene early, before the illness disrupts life (upper-year notes: within 12 weeks) · stay active · return to work
  • Predictors of long-term disability: high reported pain and disability · depression · somatization · poor coping · weak social support · unresolved legal issues · reinforced pain behaviour · job dissatisfaction · childhood sexual abuse

lectures.name: Maintaining Boundaries
lectures.title: Maintaining boundaries
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A crossing is harmless and non-exploitative; a violation exploits the patient through the relationship and harms them or their care. Sexual remarks alone count as sexual abuse under the RHPA. Sexual contact within 1 year of the relationship ending is still abuse. Report within 30 days to the professional's college, on reasonable grounds, without the patient's name unless they consent. Always offer a chaperone for intimate examinations.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Does the departure from the usual professional role harm or exploit the patient? If not, it is a boundary crossing; if it does, it is a boundary violation. Sexual abuse of a patient is always a violation, and any physician who learns of it must report.
1. Boundaries

• Boundaries: the rules that keep the professional relationship separate from every other relationship
  • Boundary crossing: a departure from usual practice that is harmless, non-exploitative, and may even support care
  • Boundary violation: harmful or potentially harmful to the patient and the care, because it exploits the patient through the doctor-patient relationship
2. The CPSO Boundary Violations policy

• The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO) requires physicians to set and keep appropriate boundaries
  • Before any examination, treatment or procedure: explain its scope and reason in advance · explain why any question about sexual matters is being asked · obtain consent
  • Always offer a third party (chaperone) for an intimate examination, whatever the gender of physician or patient · the patient may bring their own
  • Preventing violations: sensitivity to gender and culture · know patient risk factors (patients who have been abused are at higher risk of exploitation) · know your own risk factors · recognize warning signs
3. The Regulated Health Professions Act (RHPA)

• Sexual abuse of a patient means any of:
    • sexual intercourse or other physical sexual relations
    • touching of a sexual nature
    • behaviour or remarks of a sexual nature toward the patient
  • A person is a patient if any one applies: the physician charged or was paid for care · contributed to their health record · they consented to care the physician recommended · the physician prescribed them a medication needing a prescription
  • After the relationship ends: sexual contact within 1 year is still sexual abuse
    • upper-year notes add: 5 years for psychotherapy, and it may be misconduct with someone closely associated with the patient, depending on the clinical problem, type of care and emotional dependence
4. Mandatory reporting

• Same logic as child-abuse reporting: the report must be reasonable, not proven
  • Failure to report: fine of up to $25,000 and licence suspension of up to 6 months (medwiki note)

lectures.name: Delirium
lectures.title: Delirium
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Inattention with acute, fluctuating onset is delirium until proven otherwise - CAM needs features 1 and 2 plus 3 or 4. Hypoactive delirium is the commonest and is mistaken for depression. Dementia is the strongest risk factor, and delirium speeds later decline. Use benzodiazepines only for alcohol withdrawal, physostigmine for anticholinergic toxicity; otherwise low-dose antipsychotic and only for distressing symptoms. Hallucinations in delirium are mostly visual; in depression and schizophrenia mostly auditory.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with a medical cause - it is a sign that something else is wrong. Screen for it, hunt for every trigger, and treat the cause; medication only manages symptoms.
1. Approach

blocks.html: 2. Definition and subtypes

• DSM-5 criteria
    • disturbance of attention (direct, focus, sustain, shift) and awareness (orientation)
    • develops over a short time and fluctuates through the day · a change from baseline
    • plus another cognitive disturbance: memory · orientation · language · visuospatial · perception
    • not better explained by a neurocognitive disorder or coma · evidence of a medical cause, substance, medication or toxin
    • onset: the medwiki note says hours to days, the upper-year notes days to weeks (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Specifiers: substance intoxication or withdrawal · medication-induced · another medical condition · multiple causes · acute vs persistent
  • Activity subtypes
    • Hypoactive (most common, about 65%): drowsy, withdrawn, refuses to eat or for care, approaching stupor - often missed or mistaken for depression
    • Hyperactive (about 25%): hypervigilant, loud fast speech, combative, pulls at lines - can look like mania
    • Mixed (about 10%): swings between the two
  • Psychosis in about 42%: visual hallucinations most common, then auditory and tactile · poorly formed paranoid delusions · more in hyperactive
3. Who gets it

• Medical wards 10-20% · after surgery up to 50% · ICU up to 80% · elderly 10-15% at admission, 10-40% during it · up to 60% of nursing-home residents over 75
  • Risk factors: dementia (the strongest) · age over 65 · male · prior delirium · functional impairment · hearing or vision loss · polypharmacy (4 or more medications) · alcohol use disorder · dehydration, malnutrition · living in an institution
  • Up to 40% preventable
4. Causes and pathophysiology

• Common culprit drugs: benzodiazepines, diphenhydramine, tricyclics, furosemide · anticholinergics · opioids · steroids · digoxin and many more
  • Infection (lung, urine, skin, gut, central nervous system) · metabolic (sodium, calcium, glucose, thyroid, B12, thiamine, liver or kidney failure) · environment (night bloodwork, no clock or window, room changes, restraints, missing glasses and hearing aids) · structural (low oxygen, high carbon dioxide, heart attack, heart failure, stroke, seizure) · urinary retention · constipation · pain
  • An older patient's heart attack may present only as delirium
  • Pathophysiology (several hypotheses)
    • low acetylcholine (leading theory) with excess dopamine, noradrenaline and glutamate
    • neuroinflammation (peripheral inflammation activates brain cytokines) · oxidative stress · high glucocorticoids · disrupted circadian rhythm · network disconnection · aging lowers brain reserve
  • Two-way link with dementia: dementia is the strongest risk factor, and delirium raises the risk of later cognitive decline
5. Assessment at the bedside

• History: baseline · onset, course and fluctuation · sleep · hallucinations ("have you seen anything unusual?") and paranoia ("is anyone hurting you?") · collateral from family and nursing · medications
  • Observe first from the doorway: picking, pulling at lines, drowsiness, agitation
  • Orientation out of 10: year, season, month, date, day · country, province, city, building, floor
  • Attention: tap at each "A" in "SAVEAHAART" · months backwards · serial 7s · spell WORLD backwards · digit span (sources differ: medwiki says 4 digits, upper-year notes 5 - check the slides) · clock drawing
6. Delirium vs dementia vs depression
7. Management

• No drug treats delirium itself - treat the causes (medications, infection, fluids, immobility, pain, sensory deprivation)
  • Non-drug care: reorient often, clocks and calendars · family involvement · familiar items · glasses and hearing aids · mobilize early · lights and blinds open by day, dark and quiet at night · avoid restraints and lines · fewer staff changes · hydration and nutrition · stop offending drugs
  • Antipsychotics for distressing psychosis or agitation in hyperactive delirium: haloperidol (about 1 mg twice a day by mouth) or risperidone · check the QT · avoid in seizures, Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies
  • Prognosis: higher mortality (upper-year notes: 10% at 3 months, 34% at 6 months), institutionalization and dementia · may last up to 12 months · many never return to baseline

lectures.name: Cognitive Disorders in the Elderly
lectures.title: Cognitive disorders in the elderly
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Mild vs major neurocognitive disorder turns on one thing: is independence in everyday activities lost? Alzheimer: insidious, memory for new information first. Vascular: abrupt, stepwise, focal signs. Lewy body: fluctuations, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism after the dementia, REM sleep behaviour disorder. Frontotemporal: young, behaviour or language first, memory spared. Rule out depression, hypothyroidism, delirium, medications and B12 deficiency. MoCA catches mild impairment that the MMSE misses.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Two questions: does the decline cost the person their independence (major vs mild neurocognitive disorder), and which pattern of onset and symptoms does it follow (Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal)? Always look for the reversible causes first.
1. The neurocognitive disorders

• Core feature: an acquired decline in cognition · a spectrum of delirium → mild neurocognitive disorder → major neurocognitive disorder
  • Six cognitive domains: complex attention · executive function · learning and memory · language · perceptual-motor · social cognition
  • Mild neurocognitive disorder (mild cognitive impairment): modest decline in 1 or more domains · independence preserved (more effort or strategies needed)
    • 10-20% of adults over 65 · upper-year notes: 20-40% progress within 5 years · medwiki: about 10% a year, and over half stay stable or return to normal
  • Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia): significant decline in 1 or more domains that interferes with independence (at least needs help with instrumental activities such as bills and medications)
    • both: not only during a delirium · not better explained by another mental disorder such as depression
    • severity: mild = trouble with instrumental activities of daily living (shopping, housework, money, medications, transport, phone) · moderate = trouble with basic activities of daily living (dressing, eating, bathing, toileting, transferring, continence) · severe = fully dependent
  • Epidemiology: 5-7% of adults over 60 · 1-2% at 65-69, doubling every 5 years to about 30% over 85 · 65% female (longer life)
2. Normal aging vs dementia

• Normal aging: slightly slower processing · occasionally forgets but remembers later · short-term memory a little affected, long-term kept · language, abstraction and function preserved
  • Red flags: memory loss that affects function · trouble with familiar tasks, language or abstraction · disorientation · poor judgement · change in mood, behaviour or personality · loss of initiative · misplacing items
  • Risk factors: age (the biggest) · mild cognitive impairment · family history and genes · head injury · vascular risk factors · inactivity · alcohol · depression · chronic kidney disease · hearing loss · less education · social isolation - up to 40% of dementia is potentially preventable
3. Comparing the dementias

4. Workup

• Most common reversible causes: depression (pseudodementia) · hypothyroidism · delirium · medications · B12 deficiency
  • Imaging: CT rules out tumour, chronic subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke · MRI gives more detail (small tumours, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease)
  • Mnemonic for causes (upper-year notes): AV DEMENTIA - Alzheimer · vascular · dementia with Lewy bodies, depression · ethanol · medical and metabolic · endocrine, ears, eyes, environment · neurologic · toxins, tumour, trauma · infection · amnesia, apnea, autoimmune
5. Screening tests

• Describe where points were lost, and allow for deafness, blindness, low education or a second language
  • None of these tests diagnoses dementia on its own

lectures.name: Sexual Disorders and Paraphilias
lectures.title: Sexual disorders and paraphilias
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Paraphilia + (personal distress or harm to or non-consent of others) for 6 months = paraphilic disorder. Most people with paraphilias do not offend; fantasies are not illegal, acts like exhibitionism, voyeurism and pedophilia are. Psychological therapy (CBT, Good Lives Model) is first line; anti-androgens, LHRH agonists and SSRIs lower drive. Hypersexuality is not a DSM diagnosis - rule out mania, substances, brain lesions and personality disorders. Masochism = undergoing, sadism = inflicting.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

A paraphilia is an unusual sexual interest; it becomes a paraphilic disorder only when it causes the person distress or involves harm to, or the non-consent of, others. Most people with paraphilias never offend, and not every sex offender has a paraphilia.
1. Context

• Calling paraphilias a disorder is controversial - many object to pathologizing consensual adult sexual activity
  • Distressed patients still come to general mental health services; the field is a "super-subspecialty" of forensic psychiatry (psychiatry + law: court testimony, risk assessment and management of sex offenders)
  • Legality: pedophilia, voyeurism and exhibitionism are illegal only if acted on (fantasies are not illegal) · fetishism, cross-dressing and coprophilia are not illegal
2. Paraphilic disorders

• Paraphilia: any intense, persistent sexual interest other than in genital stimulation or fondling with physically mature, consenting human partners
  • Paraphilic disorder (DSM-5), over at least 6 months, either:
    • personal distress about the interest (not merely from society's disapproval), or
    • desire or behaviour involving another person's distress, injury or death, or unwilling persons or those unable to consent

rows: Touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person
Non-living objects, or a highly specific non-genital body part

blocks.html:
• Epidemiology (upper-year notes): 3.1% report at least one act of exhibitionism · 7.7% admit voyeuristic behaviour
  • Associated factors: childhood sexual abuse · attachment difficulties · social incompetence · emotional dysregulation · disinhibition from low empathy and substance use
  • Comorbidity (studied mostly in sex offenders): mood disorders · alcohol and other substance use · personality disorders
  • Paraphilias are not generally linked to serious sexual violence, but up to 80% of sexual murderers have a history of paraphilic behaviour (upper-year notes)
3. Treatment of paraphilic disorders

• Psychological treatment is the gold standard
    • CBT: social skills training · cognitive restructuring · victim empathy
    • Good Lives Model: strengths-based - builds the skills to meet normal human needs in personally meaningful, socially acceptable ways
  • Biological (evidence mostly from convicted offenders, and limited)
    • historically surgical castration
    • anti-androgens (cyproterone acetate)
    • luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists (triptorelin, goserelin)
    • SSRIs to lower libido
4. Sex addiction (problematic hypersexuality)

• Also called sexual compulsivity or impulsivity · not a DSM-5 diagnosis - usually coded as a paraphilic or other specified sexual disorder
  • Problematic when: loss of control over fantasies, urges and behaviour plus adverse consequences or personal distress
  • Research definition: 7 or more orgasms ("total sexual outlets") a week · upper-year notes add: for 6 months, 1-2 hours a day
  • Three models: addiction · compulsivity (like obsessive-compulsive disorder) · impulsivity · in each the behaviour regulates emotional states
  • Rule out and treat what mimics or drives it
    • medical: temporal lobe lesions · brain injury · hypergonadal states · pituitary dysfunction
    • substances: alcohol · amphetamines · cocaine · cannabis
    • bipolar disorder · psychotic disorders
    • personality disorders: antisocial · borderline
  • Management follows the mechanism thought to drive the behaviour · lower impulsivity predicts a better outcome (upper-year notes)

lectures.name: Management of Cognitive Disorders and Dementia
lectures.title: Management of cognitive disorders and dementia
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Look for unmet needs and medical causes, and use non-drug approaches first - antipsychotics only for severe agitation, aggression or psychosis, or a safety risk. Citalopram is the best-supported antidepressant; risperidone the best-supported antipsychotic for BPSD. Lewy body dementia: be wary of antipsychotics, use cholinesterase inhibitors. Suspected dementia must be reported to the MTO; elder abuse must be reported only in long-term care. Wandering, undressing and vocalizing rarely respond to drugs.

blocks.title: Draft
blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

There is no cure, so the aim is function, safety, comfort and dignity for the patient and support for the caregiver. For behavioural and psychological symptoms, find the cause and try non-drug approaches first; medication is for severe or dangerous symptoms.
1. General management of dementia

• Alliance with patient and family → disclose the diagnosis and prognosis, plan treatment, raise safety and legal issues
  • Safety: the 3 Fs - fire, flood, falls · driving · medications · home
  • Legal duties
    • must report to the Ministry of Transportation (MTO) when dementia is suspected
    • no legal duty to report elder abuse - unless it happens in a long-term care home
  • Future planning: power of attorney · placement decisions (long-term care waiting lists are long) · advance care planning
  • Community supports: home care (Ontario Health atHome) · Alzheimer Society · Meals on Wheels (especially after an MTO report for someone who lives alone or with a non-driving partner) · blister packs and medication delivery · day programs · caregiver support
  • Risk reduction for further decline: nutrition · exercise · hearing · sleep · cognitive training · social engagement · frailty · vascular risk factors · minimize anticholinergics and polypharmacy
  • Goals of medication: delay progression and functional decline · control symptoms · comfort · quality of life and dignity · treat comorbidities such as depression · support the caregiver
2. Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD)

• About 90% of people with dementia have them · they arise from the brain disease, not from earlier psychiatric illness
    • affective: depression · anxiety · elation or disinhibition · apathy
    • behavioural: irritability · agitation or aggression · pacing, wandering · sleep disturbance · sexual disinhibition · vocalizing
    • psychotic: hallucinations · delusions (paranoid or misidentification)
  • By dementia type: frontotemporal → behavioural symptoms · Lewy body → visual hallucinations · vascular → depression and apathy · Alzheimer → delusions, mostly persecutory
  • "Responsive behaviours": every behaviour expresses something meaningful - a response to the person's surroundings, needs or misread information
  • Causes: unmet needs (pain, thirst, hunger, toileting) · medical illness or delirium · medications · lower distress tolerance · learned behaviour · environment (over- or under-stimulating) · caregiver stress or lack of training
  • Consequences: earlier long-term care · hospitalization · emotional and financial strain
3. Assessment and approach

• DICE: Describe · Investigate · Create · Evaluate · also ABC (antecedent, behaviour, consequence) and the PIECES caregiver training
  • Rating scales: Neuropsychiatric Inventory · Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory · Brief Agitation Rating Scale · Pittsburgh Agitation Scale, among others
4. Non-drug management (always first)

• Reduce isolation, stimulate the senses, relax: talking and singing · family videos · pet and music therapy · multisensory (Snoezelen) room · aromatherapy · bright light · massage and touch
  • Engagement: recreation · walking programs · group exercise
  • Behaviour therapy: reward behaviours incompatible with the problem one · cueing · staff training
  • Practical techniques (upper-year notes): priming (predictable routine, familiar objects) · miming (communicate in more than one way at once) · timing (time of day, pacing) · environment (quiet, daylight) · gentle persuasion
  • Limits: modest effect · weaker for aggression and psychosis
  • Hard to treat with any drug: wandering · undressing · vocalizing · inappropriate urination · hoarding · eating non-food items
5. Medication for BPSD
• Older brains need lower doses and are more sensitive to side effects · minimize polypharmacy

• By type: frontotemporal → trazodone and SSRIs (citalopram) · Lewy body → cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine first for fluctuation, agitation and psychosis · extremely sensitive to antipsychotics (sources differ: the medwiki lecture note allows quetiapine or clozapine, its dementia with Lewy bodies note says do not use antipsychotics - check the slides)
  • Severe cases: anticonvulsants or short-acting benzodiazepines (upper-year notes)
  • The upper-year notes list atypical antipsychotics or antidepressants first; the medwiki note puts antidepressants first unless there is psychosis, aggression or risk (check the slides)

lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Cholinesterase inhibitors for mild to severe Alzheimer, Parkinson disease dementia and Lewy body dementia; memantine only for moderate to severe Alzheimer. Cholinergic side effects: gut upset most often, but watch for bradycardia and syncope - a heart rate under 50 or heart block is a contraindication. No role in mild cognitive impairment. Titrate every 4 weeks, never stop abruptly, and taper by halves every 4 weeks. Loss of effect after years is progression, not a reason to switch.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Two classes: cholinesterase inhibitors raise acetylcholine, memantine damps excess glutamate. They slow decline modestly but cure nothing - the art is choosing the right diagnosis and stage, titrating slowly, and knowing when to switch or stop.
1. The two classes

blocks.alt: dementia drugs (AChE inhibitors vs. NMDA antagonists).png
blocks.cap: Cholinesterase inhibitors block acetylcholine breakdown in the synapse; memantine blocks the NMDA glutamate receptor

rows: Block acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks acetylcholine into acetate and choline → more acetylcholine in the synapse (not reuptake inhibition)
Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist → less activation by the excess glutamate of dementia → less calcium-driven cell damage

Alzheimer · mixed Alzheimer and vascular · Parkinson disease dementia · dementia with Lewy bodies · vascular alone: possible (sources differ: the lecture note and upper-year notes allow some benefit, the medwiki vascular dementia note says not for isolated vascular dementia - check the slides)
Alzheimer only · not frontotemporal or pure vascular dementia
Mild to severe dementia - all three equally effective, none superior

Cholinergic excess (DUMBBELLS): diarrhea, nausea and other gut effects (most common) · urinary incontinence · miosis · bronchospasm · bradycardia, syncope · emesis · lethargy · lacrimation · salivation · also insomnia, nightmares, muscle cramps, agitation, seizures
Usually well tolerated · dizziness · headache · constipation · also agitation or sleepiness, hypertension, hallucinations
Heart rate under 50, sick sinus, left bundle branch block, third-degree heart block · active peptic ulcer · severe asthma or COPD · epilepsy · delirium · angle-closure glaucoma · very low weight
Severe renal impairment: lower the dose
Donepezil: liver (half-life about 70 hours) · galantamine: liver (± kidney) · rivastigmine: kidney per medwiki, hydrolysis per upper-year notes (check the slides)

blocks.html:
• Combination of both classes: the medwiki note says they can be combined, its Alzheimer note and the upper-year notes say the evidence is insufficient (sources differ - check the slides)
  • No evidence in mild cognitive impairment - prescribe only for confirmed major neurocognitive disorder, but not so late that the neurons are already lost
2. Dosing

rows: 8 mg a day (or 4 mg twice a day)
4.5 mg twice a day · max 6 mg twice a day

blocks.html:
• Titrate very slowly: raise the dose about every 4 weeks · a trial takes 3-6 months (about twice as slow as antidepressants)
  • Memantine: the upper-year notes raise it by 5 mg weekly, reaching 10 mg twice a day by week 4 (sources differ: the medwiki note raises all these drugs monthly - check the slides)
  • Never stop abruptly
3. Monitoring and expectations

• Before and during: cognition (MoCA or MMSE, serial) · function and behaviour · patient and caregiver report · ECG, heart rate, blood pressure · weight
  • Expect modest benefit: they slow decline rather than stop it, so scores still fall
    • upper-year notes: cognitive gains peak at about 6 months and return to baseline by 9-12 months · global measures peak by 3 months
    • may prevent or ease neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression, apathy)
  • Side effects are usually mild - do not add another drug to treat them · try a lower dose or a shorter half-life agent
4. Switching and stopping

blocks.html:
• Stop when: dementia worsens significantly over 6 months on treatment · no meaningful benefit · severe or end-stage dementia (total care) · intolerable side effects · poor adherence or monitoring not possible
  • Taper: halve the dose every 4 weeks (twice as slow as SSRIs) · watch for rapid cognitive decline or responsive behaviours
